full_judgment:
Borhanuddin J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 12-3-2002 (decree sired on 18-3-2002) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 4th Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 93 of 2001 dismissing the suit under-Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The appellant as plaintiff instituted Title suit No. 93 of 2001 in the Court of learned Sub-ordinate. Judge, 4th Court, Khulna, impleading the respondents as defendants for a declaration that the preliminary decree dated 30-2-1997 and final decree dated 12-3-2001 passed in Artha Rin Suit No. 35 of 1996 covering the property of the, plaintiff was illegal, collusive, inoperative and not binding upon him.

3. The plaintiff's case, in short, is that, the plaintiff availed loan facility from the branch of the defendant No. 1-Bank, and still there is transaction between the plaintiff and the said branch of the defendant No. 1 but the plaintiff did not mortgage his land against the said loan and did not make himself guarantor for any loan sanctioned in favour of any other person. On 15-7-2001, the plaintiff came to know from an employee of the defendant No. 1 at Kapi-Imunirhat that the defendant No. 1 obtained an ex-parte decree against him. On hearing the same, the plaintiff rushed to Khulna and applied for inspection through an advocate and on 22-7-2001 for the first time came to know about the said ex-parte judgment and decree. The plaintiff has already applied for the certified copy of the judgment and decree but hurriedly filed the instant suit apprehending that in the meantime, the defendant No. 1 Bank may take action against him. It has also been stated that in the Artha Rin Suit No. 35 of 1996 this plaintiff was impleaded as defendant No. 3. Though the defendant No. 3 of the present suit is that son of plaintiff's full brother but they are living separately. The plaintiff has no manner of relationship with the defendant No. 3. As both of them are co-sharers in the same jama a single khatian is prepared in their names but they separated their lands by amicable partition since long. The plaintiff has no connection with the business of the defendant No. 3 Decree in Artha Rin Suit No. 35 of 1996 obtained in collusion with the defendant No. 3 and some dishonest employees of the defendant No. 1 by creating forged document in the name of the plaintiff. It has been further stated that no notice was served upon the plaintiff. Registered notice dated 20-9-1995 was also not served upon the plaintiff and he did not sign the acknowledgement receipt. The plaintiff is a simple cultivator and most of the time resides in his house. Notice of the final decree was received by the defendant No. 3 but he did not inform the plaintiff about the notice. Everything was done keeping the plaintiff in dark. It is true that there is a loan in the name of the plaintiff with the defendant No. 1 but the said loan has no relation with the loan amount decreed in Artha Rin Suit No. 35 of 1996. The cause of action arose on 22-7-2001 when the plaintiff for the first time came to know about the ex-parte judgment and decree dated 12-3-2001 passed in Artha Rin Suit No. 35 of 1996 as such filed the suit for declaration.

4. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying material allegations made in the plaint and contending inter-alia that the plaintiff applied to the defendant No. 1-bank for sanctioning loan in favour of defendant No. 2 M/s. PP Shrimp Production Firm owned and managed by his nephew, defendant No. 3. The defendant No. 1 sanctioned loan of Taka 2,70,000 vide advise letter dated 21-3-1990 and as per terms of the advise letter, this plaintiff executed and registered mortgage deed No. 1662 dated 5-4-1990 in favour of the defendant No. 1 and also executed all charge documents. The plaintiff also executed a deed of guarantee undertaking the responsibility to repay the loan amount in default by the defendants No. 2 and 3. Thereafter, on 23-2-1991, the defendant No. 1 against sanctioned a short-term loan of Taka 2,07,000 and rescheduled the earlier loan amount pursuant to an application filed by the plaintiff. This time also the plaintiff executed all charge documents and executed personal guarantee to secure the loan amount. After the expiry period as per terms of the advice letter, the defendants No. 2 and 3 did not repay the loan amount. This defendant requested them orally and also in writing to repay the loan amount but they did not pay heed to it. Then the defendant No. 1 issued legal notice but no response. In this circumstances, this defendant being plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 35 of 1996 to recover the loan amount. Though notice was served upon the defendants but the present plaintiff and his nephew (defendants No. 1 and 3 in Title Suit No. 35 of 1996) did not contest the suit. The Artha Rin Adalat preliminary decreed the suit ex-parte on 1-3-1997 and finally decreed on 12-4-2000. The plaintiff of the present suit executed deed of guarantee as personal guarantor and deposited the same to the defendant No. 1. He duly received the letters, legal notice and also notice of the Title Suit No. 35 of 1996 but intentionally refrained from contesting the suit in collusion with his nephew, the defendant No. 3, to deceive the defendant No. 1. The plaintiff and the defendant No. 3 has availed the entire loan amount but still filed the present suit in collusion with each other to defraud this defendant. It has been further stated that pursuant to sections 5-7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990, no judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat can be challenged in any court of authority excepting filing appeal. With such averments the defendant No. 1 prayed for dismissal of the suit with cost.

5. After the suit was registered, the defendant No. 1 made an application under Order VII Rule 11 (Kha) of the Code of Civil Procedure for dismissal of the suit on the ground that it was not maintainable under sections 5-7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990. After hearing the parties, the learned Joint District Judge, Khulna, allowed the application and dismissed the suit as not maintainable vide Order No. 8 dated 12-3-2002. The order followed by a decree drawn on 18-3-2002. Against the decree the plaintiff preferred the instant appeal.

6. Mr M Quamrul Haque Siddiqui the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant submits that the jurisdiction of civil court ousted by express provisions in section 6(1) of the Ain, 1990, is not applicable for a decree obtained by practicing fraud. He submits that the plaintiff of this suit was impleaded as defendant No. 3 in the Artha Rin Suit No. 35 of 1996 but he was not aware of the proceedings of the suit, as no summons or notices were served upon him. In elaborating his submission, the learned Advocate submits that section 6 of the Ain, 1990, has ousted jurisdiction of all courts and authorities save as prescribed by appeal under section or by filing application under Order IX Rule 13 by depositing 50% of the decreetal amount. For appeal also 50% of the decreetal dues must be deposited. Limitation is 30 days. There is no scope for condemnation of delay. The learned Advocate submits that once decree is passed and time limit is over, does not matter whether the decree was obtained by forgery, misrepresentation, false personation, suppression of fact, misleading the court or use of any other mala fide device, no process or procedure of justice can sit upon the decree so obtained. He admits such deterrent provision has been made to prevent loan default culture, but now a days it appears that by taking advantage of such deterrent law, forged, fraudulent documents are being used, fraudulent and mala fide devices are being practiced for obtaining an 'immune' decree from Artha Rin Adalat as a tool to oppress persons and fetching unlawful gain out of such decree. In view of the same the learned Advocate submits that time has ripen enough to examine the extent of 'immunity' given to a decree by section 6 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990. The learned advocate next submits that Writ Jurisdiction or Appellate Jurisdiction or jurisdiction under Order IX Rule 13 of the code of Civil Procedure or the like is not the forum for deciding an allegation of (a) using forged document (b) practicing fraud by forgery in effecting service (c) misrepresentation of fact (d) other malafide and fraudulent devices in obtaining decree from Artha Rin Adalat, which is conveniently used as a tool to oppress persons in distress. As such, he submits that in spite of express ouster of jurisdiction by Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990, civil court should have jurisdiction to examine the allegations of forgery, fraud, misrepresentation in obtaining decree from Artha Rin Adalat, which renders such decree void ability.

7. Relating to jurisdiction of civil court ousted by express provisions of the other statutes the learned Advocate referred to the case of Yakub Ali vs Arabjan Bibi, reported in 5 DLR 1; the case of Fazlur Rnhman vs Abdul Jabbar Jamader, reported in 7 DLR 49; the case of Sarat Chandra Majumder vs SM Hara Sundari De, reported in 10 DLR 289; the case of Syed Tarab-uddin vs Kali Kumar Saha Roy, reported in 10 DLR 634; the case of Abdur Rouf vs Abdul Hamid Khan, reported in 17 DLR (SC) 515; the case of Shams-uddin Khan vs Shamsuzzaman, reported in 22 DLR 655; the case of Noor Mohammad vs Moulavi Moinuddin Ahmed, reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 342 and also the case of Shahidullah (Md) vs Abdus Sobhan Taslukder, reported in 49 DLR 248.

8. Relating to ouster of jurisdiction as contemplated in section 6 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990, the learned Advocate referred to the case of China Arjumand Banu vs Rupali Bank, reported in 14 BLD 321 the case of Harun Or Rashid vs Rupali Bank, reported in 50 DLR 170 and the case of Md Mozammel Hoq vs Sonali Bank, reported in 15 BLD (AD) 35. The learned Advocate mainly relied upon the case of Md Mozammel Hoq vs Sonali Bank, reported in 15 BLD (AD) 35.

9. Mr Zafarullah Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the respondents, on the other hand, in support of the impugned judgment and decree, submits that the decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat was challenged in the instant suit which is expressly barred under section 6(1) of the Artha Rin Ain, 1990. In support of his submission, Mr Chowdhury referred to the case of Nurul Islam (Md) vs Agrani Bank, reported in 49 DLR (AD) 135; the case of Delowar Hossain vs Janata Bank, reported in 55 DLR 588 and the case of Gazi M Tawfic vs Agrani bank, reported in 54 DLR (AD) 6.

10. Heard the learned Advocates at length; perused the impugned judgment and decree. From the submissions of the learned Advocates it appears that only question is to be resolved whether Title Suit No. 93 of 2001 instituted by the plaintiff-appellant praying for a declaration that the preliminary decree and the final decree passed in Artha Rin Suit No. 35 of 1996 was illegal, collusive, fraudulent, in-operative and not binding upon the plaintiff, is maintainable or not.

11. section 6 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 provides that the proceeding, order, judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat cannot be questioned before any court or any other authority, but section 6 has been made applicable subject to the provisions of section 7. sections 6 and 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990, runs as follows:—

৬।“ অর্থ ঋন আদালতের সিদ্ধান্ত চুড়ান্ত-(১) ধারা ৭ এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, অর্থ ঋন আদালতের কার্যধারা, আদেশ, রায় ও ডিক্রী সম্পর্কে কোন আদালত বা অন্য কোন কর্তৃপক্ষের নিকট প্রশ্ন উত্থাপন করা যাইবে না। (২) উপ-ধারা(১) এ যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, কোন অর্থ ঋন আদালত কর্তৃক বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে প্রদত্ত কোন একতরফা ডিক্রী রদ করার জন্য বিবাদী Code of Civil Procedure, 1908(Act of 1908) এর order IX এর rule 13 এর বিধান মোতাবেক আদালতে দরখাস্ত করিতে চাহিলে তাহাকে তাহার বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রিকৃত অর্থের অন্তত, অর্ধেক অর্থ বা উহার সমপরিমান অর্থের ব্যাংক জামানত দরখাস্তের সহিত আদালতে জমা করিতে হইবে এবং উক্ত রুপ জমা করা না হইলে তাহার দরখাস্ত গ্রহনযোগ্য হইবে না।”

৭. আপীল-(১) কোন ব্যক্তি অর্থ ঋন আদালতের কোন রায় বা ডিক্রী দ্বারা ক্ষুব্দ হইলে তিনি উক্ত রায় বা ডিক্রী প্রদানের তারিখ হইতে ৩০ দিনের মধ্যে হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে আপীল করিতে পারিবেন”

তবে, শর্ত থাকে যে, অর্থ ঋন আদালতের কোন অন্তবর্তী আদেশের বিরুদ্ধে কোন আপীল রায়ের করা যাইবে না।

(২) ধারা ৬(২) এর অধীন দায়েরকৃত দরখাস্তের উপর অর্থ ঋন আদালত কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত চুড়ান্ত আদেশের বিরুদ্ধে কোন বিবাদী-

(অ) আপীল দায়ের করিতে ইচ্চুক হইলে বা

(আ) আপীল দায়ের না করিয়া মূল মামলার রায় বা ডিক্রীর বিরুদ্ধে আপীল দায়ের করিতে ইচ্চুক হইলে-

তিনি উক্ত ধারার অধীন জমাকৃত অর্থ বাদ দিয়া মূল মামলায় ডিক্রীকৃত অবশিষ্ট অর্থের অন্ততঃ অর্ধেক অর্থ ডিক্রী প্রদানকারী আদালতের নিকট জমা করিয়া, উক্ত চুড়ান্ত আদেশ প্রদানের তারিখ হইতে ৩০ দিনের মধ্যে, হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে আপীল করিতে পারিবেন।

(৩) অর্থ ঋন আদালতের কোন রায় বা ডিক্রীর বিরুদ্ধে কোন বিবাদী আপীল দায়ের করিতে ইচ্ছুক হইলে এবং তিনি উক্ত রায় বা ডিক্রীর বিরুদ্ধে-

(অ) ধারা ৬(২) এর অধীন দরখাস্ত না করিয়া থাকিলে, তাহার বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রীকৃত অর্থের অন্ততঃ অর্ধেক অর্থ,

(আ) ধারা ৬(২) এর অধীন দরখাস্ত এবং উপ-ধারা (২)(ক) এর অধীন আপীল করিয়া থাকিলে, উক্ত ধারা ৬(২) এবং উপ-ধারা (২)(ক) এর অধীন জমাকৃত অর্থই বাদ দিয়া মূল মামলায় ডিক্রীকৃত অবশিষ্ট অর্থের অন্ততঃ অধেৃক অর্থই ডিক্রী প্রদানকারী আদালতে জমা করিয়া উপ-ধারা(১) এ নির্ধারিত সময়ের মধ্যে হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে আপীল দায়ের করিতে পারিবেন।

(৪) কোন বিবাদী উপ-ধারা (২) এবং (৩) এ নির্ধারিত অর্থ ডিক্রী প্রদানকারী আদালতে জমা না করিলে উক্ত বিবাদীর আপীল গ্রহন যোগ্য হইবে না।

12. In the case of Sultana Jute Mills Ltd vs Agrani Bank, reported in 14 BLD (AD) 196= 46 DLR (AD) 174, our Apex Court held:—

"Revisional Jurisdiction of the High Court Division is provided for in section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in making under section 6 the proceeding, order, judgment and decree of an Artha Rin Adalat not amenable to interference by any court or authority. The aim of the Adalat Act was to create departure from the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 7, it may be said, was meant to be an exception to this complete ouster of interference. An exception has been made in respect of a judgment and decree in section 7(1). Another exception has been made in respect of a final order under Order IX Rule 13 CPC. In both the cases, appeal will be to the High Court Division. There is room for argument that both the appellate and revisional powers of interference with any "order" interlocutory or otherwise, is expressly barred by section 6. The proviso to section 7(1) barring an appeal against an. interlocutory order has been provided for only as a measure of abundant caution. In other words, section 7 is an exception to that ouster. The exception cannot render the ouster provision nugatory".

13. In the case of Gazi M Tawfic vs Agrani Bank, reported in 54 DLR (AD) 6, our Apex Court held;

"Law is now settled since special provision of appeal has been made against the decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, no application under Article 102 lies against such judgment and decree." However, as we mentioned earlier that the learned Advocate for the appellant mainly relied upon the case of Md Mozammel vs Sonali Bank, reported in 15 BLD (AD) 35, wherein our appellate Division held; "If the petitioner's allegation of non-service of summons of the suit is correct, his remedy of a separate suit is not barred provided his remedies under Artha Rin Adalat stood at the time of filing of the suit for no default of his own."

14. The learned Advocate, for the appellant submits that the main allegation of the plaintiff-appellant was that the summon of Title suit No. 35 of 1996 was not served upon him. We have carefully gone through the judgment reported in 15 BLD (AD) 35. Said Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal arose against the judgment and order of this Division rejecting the prayer for stay of the proceedings of the execution case. Facts as stated in the said Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal is that the petitioner was a resident of. Dhaka and the Mortgage Suit was filed in Rajshahi and he received no notice of the suit. But in the instant case, i.e. Title Suit No. 93 of 2001, the plaintiff stated in paragraph No. 2 of his plaint that “১নং বিবাদী অগ্রনী ব্যাংক কপিলমুনি শাখার থেকে বাদীর নিজ নামে পূর্বে লোন নিয়েছিলে��। অদ্যাবধি উক্ত শাখা থেকে টাকা লেন করে আসছেন।”

15. Admittedly, defendant No. 3 against whom the forgery was alleged, is the son of the plaintiffs full brother i.e. nephew of the plaintiff. It appears from the plaint that the address of both the plaintiff and the defendant No. 3 are same. So, the facts and circumstances of the case, reported in 15 BLD, is distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the case in hand.

16. It appears from the facts of the case of Nurul Islam (Md) vs Agrani Bank, reported in 49 DLR (AD) 135 that the Money Suit No. 9 of 1992 filed in the Court of Artha Rin Adalat, Jamalpur, was decreed ex-parte on 30 August, 1993 whereupon the petitioner filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting-aside the judgment and decree on the ground of 'fraud'. The same was rejected by the trial court on the ground of maintainability which was also affirmed by this division; against which the petitioner moved before the Appellate Division, wherein our Apex Court held:—

"Learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, contends that when the petitioner-defendant challenged the ex-parte decree on the ground of fraud his application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is quite maintainable. We do not find any substance in this contention, for the Artha Rin Adalat specifically provides for only 2 remedies against an ex-parte decree. It is either by an application or by an appeal; but in both the cases deposit of 50% decreetal amount is necessary. To avoid this deposit, it appears, the petitioner has sought a short cut by invoking section 151 CPC which is not applicable in such a situation. The application under section 151 is found to have been rightly dismissed. This petition is dismissed."

17. The learned Advocate for the appellant submits that section 6 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 has ousted jurisdiction of all courts and authorities save as prescribed by appeal under section 7 or by filing application under Order IX, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure on depositing 50% of the decreetal dues. For appeal also 50% of the decreetal dues must be deposited. Limitation is 30 days. There is no scope for condonation of delay. By taking advantage of such deterrent law some unscrupulous people has started abusing the law by way of creating forged, fraudulent documents and by obtaining decree with those forged and fraudulent document are fetching unlawful gain out of such decree. As such, the learned Advocate submits that in spite of express ouster Jurisdiction, Civil Court should have Jurisdiction to examine the allegations of fraud, forgery, misrepresentation in obtaining decree from Artha Rin Adalat, which renders such decree void bonito.

18. The word 'jurisdiction' does not connote form or manner in which the act is to be done but relates to the power, the scope, and the ambit of authority. It is only by virtues of statutes that jurisdiction is conferred on courts or taken away from them. In the absence of clear provisions, where the jurisdiction of a court in certain matters is statutory, the court however admirable its intentions, is not entitled to go outside those provisions and in effect legislate for itself.

19. The plain meaning rule must mean that when on construing the words of a statute it is found that the words admit of only one meaning, it is the duty of the court to give effect that meaning irrespective of consequence. In the case of Jamalus Sattar vs Badrul Hoque, reported in 16 DLR 593, their lordships held:—"However unjust, arbitrary or inconvenient the meaning is conveyed may be, it must receipt its full effect. When once the meaning is plain, it is no the province of a court to scan its wisdom or its policy."

<u>20. In the facts and circumstances of the Case and the discussion made: hereinabove based on the decisions referred above, we are of the view that since Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990, is a special statute and section 6 of the Ain, 1990, expressly ousted the jurisdiction of any court or authority relating to any proceeding, order, judgment and decree subject to the provisions of section 7 of the Ain, 1990. Title Suit No. 93 of 2001 filed by the plaintiff-appellant in the court of Sub-ordinate Judge, 4th Court, Khulna for a declaration that the judgment and decree passed by Artha Rin Adalat in Artha Rin Suit No. 35 of 1996 was illegal, collusive, inoperative and no binding upon him, is not maintainable in law.</u>

21. For the reasons stated above, we hold that the learned Joint District Judge, Khulna, legally passed the judgment and decree dated 12-3-2002 (decree signed on 18-3-2002) in Title Suit No. 93 of 2001 dismissing the suit as not maintainable under Order VII, Rule 11 (Kha) of the Code of Civil Procedure and there is nothing to interfere with the

22. In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree dated 12-3-2002 (decree signed on 18-3-2002) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 4th Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 93 of 2001 is hereby affirmed.

However, there will be no order as to costs. Send down the lower Court's record at once.

End.

lawyer:
Awsafer Rahman, Advocate with MG Mahmud Shahin and M Shaeedul Islam—For the Petitioner. 
Md Kamruzzaman, Advocate with Nur-a-Alam—For the Respondent No. 2 Bank. 
Golam Arshad with Md Rafiqul Imam, Advocates—For Respondent No. 3 (Auction Purchaser)
parties:
AB Mannaf Sheikh (Md) ------- Petitioner
Vs
1st Joint District Judge Court and Artha Rin Adalat and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Hoque J: On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh this Rule Nisi has been issued at the instance of the petitioner calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned orders, dated 3-10-2011 and 9-10-2011 passed by the respondent No. 1, 1st Joint District Judge Court and Artha Rin Adalat, Faridpur in Artha Rin Execution Case No. 1 of 2010, allegedly rejecting the application dated 26-9-2011 and 27-9-2011 filed by the petitioner for staying the auction process and accepting the auction bid of one Khaja Abdus Sattar (Annexure-B) should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect, and/or why such other or further order or orders as this Court may deem fit and proper, should not be passed.

2. Facts of the petitioner's case, in brief, are that the respondent No. 2 Bank as plaintiff instituted Artha Rin Suit No. 13 of 2007 before the Artha Rin Adalat, Faridpur, against the petitioner for recovery of Taka 3, 90,882 granted as loan. The said Artha Rin suit was heard ex-parte in the absence of the petitioner and the respondent No. 1, Court decreed the suit ex-parte in favour of the respondent No. 2 Bank by its judgment and decree dated 12-5-2009 and by the said decree the petitioner was directed to make payment of the decretal amount to the Bank within 40 days from the date of the order. The petitioner having failed to repay the same, the respondent No. 2 Bank put the said decree into execution by filing Artha Rin Execution Case No. 1 of 2010 in the Court of Artha Rin Adalat, Faridpur on 4-2-2010. The petitioner on coming to know about the filing of the Execution case filed an application on 29-9-2010 seeking time to pay the Bank's dues stating that the petitioner earlier paid Taka 50,000 before the Artha Rin Adalat which was fixed for hearing amongst other dates and finally on 20-6-2011. But on the date fixed the said application was rejected by the court refusing time to the petitioner to make payment of the outstanding dues to the bank. Thereafter, the petitioner again deposited Taka 50,000 with the respondent No. 2 Bank towards repayment of the loan on 26-9-2011 and filed an application before the Artha Rin Adalat praying for three months, time to pay the rest of the amount. On the following date on 27-9-2011 the petitioner filed another application before the executing Court praying for stay of the auction process and also to be granted time for repayment of the loan. The Artha Rin Adalat after hearing the application mentioned above rejected the same by its order dated 3-10-2011 observing that the petitioner is unnecessarily delaying the disposal of the execution case and proceeded to hold the auction on 3-10-2011. Subsequently, the Artha Rin Adalat accepted the auction bid of one Khaja Abdus Sattar in rejecting the prayer of the petitioner. The petitioner contends that by this time the petitioner by various installments in total deposited Taka 1,15,000 with the respondent No. 2, Bank. At this stage the petitioner moved this court by filing this application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the Peoples Republic of Bangladesh and obtained the present rule and stay. Further case of the petitioner is that after acceptance of the auction bid the petitioner filed an application before the Artha Rin Adalat under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure ("Code") on 16-11-2011 by depositing 5% of the bid money for payment to the auction purchaser praying for allowing the petitioner to get the mortgaged property released/redeemed upon payment the outstanding dues to the bank. But the court fixed on 20-11-2011 for hearing the application allowing time to the decree holder to file written objection. On 20-11-2011 the petition was heard and upon hearing the Artha Rin Adalat rejected the same, not on merit but only observing that since the matter is pending before the High Court Division the petition is not at all considerable at this stage. Thereafter, the petitioner filed another application on 4-1-2012 under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code praying for set-ting aside the auction sale. The said petition was heard on 5-1-2012 and after hearing, the court rejected the same as the proceeding has been stayed by the High Court Division in this instant application.

3. On the other hand, the respondent No. 2 Bank and auction purchaser as added respondent No. 3 contested the Rule by filing separate affidavits-in-opposition. The case of the respondent No. 2 Bank, in short, is that the petitioner was granted a loan of Taka 2,00,000 on 11-8-2002 and against the loan the petitioner executed relevant charge documents, promissory note and created mortgage of his landed property as security by a deed of mortgage No. 5026 and also executed a power of attorney on 4-8-2002 authorizing the Bank to sell the mortgaged property. The petitioner, however, failed to pay the outstanding dues within the stipulated time in spite of repeated demands and reminders of the Bank. The Bank finding no alternative was compelled to sell the property under section 12 of the Artha Rin Ain, 2003 ("Act") and published tender notice in "The Daily Jugantor" on 19-8-2005. But no bidder participated in the tender. As a result the Bank filed the Artha Rin Suit No. 13 of 2007 before the Artha Rin Adalat, Faridpur. The Artha Rin Adalat decreed the suit against the petitioner on 18-5-2009. The petitioner having failed to repay the total amount as per decree passed by the Adalat, the respondent Bank put the decree into execution by filing Execution Case No. 1 of 2010 in the Artha Rin Adalat. In the process of execution, the mortgaged property was put into auction by the court and in the auction sale, the intended buyers submitted "Sealed quotation" and amongst the bidders the bid of respondent No. 3 became highest and upon compliance of relevant provision of law the respondent No. 3's bid was accepted by the Adalat. Thereafter, entire bid money has been deposited by the respondent No. 3 to the Court and, as such, there has been no irregularity and illegality in holding auction of the mortgaged property. Hence, the Respondent's submit, the present Rule is liable to be discharged.

4. The added respondent No. 3, auction purchaser's case, in short, is that the respondent No. 3 is a lawful purchaser of the mortgaged property in auction and he has paid the entire bid money and, as such, has acquired the lawful right in the purchased property. The respondent No. 3 affirms that he has participated in the auction and has become the highest bidder. The court accepted his bid by its order dated 9-10-2011. Submitting that there is no illegality in the impugned order passed by the court, the respondent No. 3 stresses that the petitioner had remedy against the auction held under rules 89 and 90 of Order XXI of the Code but he having failed to avail the same, this petition is not tenable in law and the Rule is liable to be discharged.

5. Mr Awsafur Rahman, the learned advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that on 26-9-2011 the date fixed for holding auction, the petitioner appeared in court and filed an application praying 3 months time to pay the bank's dues stating that he has paid Taka 50,000 to the bank out of the decretal amount. The said application was kept in file and the court fixed 3-10-2011 for hearing and order. On the following day the petitioner again filed an application praying for time to pay the decretal amount and staying execution proceedings stating the situation and expressing his willingness to liquidate the bank's outstanding dues. The court kept the same in record and fixed 3-10-2011 for hearing the same and upon hearing rejected the same stating that the petitioner with an intention to cause delay in disposing the case filed the application. By its order dated 03-10-2011 the Court fixed date on 9-10-2011 for hearing the decree holder bank giving it an opportunity to raise objections, if any, regarding auction and for order. On that date the petitioner filed an application praying stay of the execution proceedings which was rejected by the Court on the ground that a similar application filed by the petitioner had already been rejected on 3- 10-2011.Consequentially, the Court accepted the bid of the respondent No. 3 auction purchaser given that his bid was found to be the highest and directed the respondent No. 3 to pay the balance bid money by 20-10-2011.

6. It is also argued that the decree was passed ex-parte and the petitioner had no knowledge about filing of the suit but he only came to know when auction notice was published in the daily news-paper. It is also submitted that the petitioner availed loan of Taka 2,00,000 out of which the petitioner paid Taka 1,15,000 to the bank on different dates. Had the court allowed time to the petitioner, the petitioner would have been able to make payment of the balance amount to the bank and, as such, the impugned orders are bad in law. He further submits that the property in question is the homestead of the petitioner and the petitioner will be homeless if the property is sold by the bank. It is noted that in addition to the applications of 16-11-2011 and 4-1-2012, the petitioner filed an application on 13-2-2012 seeking a direction upon the bank to accept the balance decretal amount from the petitioner. Upon hearing the court rejected the said application as the Execution proceedings has been stayed by this Court. Mr Rahman, therefore, referring to the various applications and orders of the Artha Rin Adalat annexed to the petition, supplementary affidavit and affidavit-in-opposition submits that the petitioner from the date of auction onwards approached the Court in various ways to get the property released upon payment of the balance out-standing dues to bank. Referring to the provisions of sections 38, 45, 49 and 57 of the Act and Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code he further argued that the court had ample scope to consider the prayer and approach of the petitioner under sections 38 and 45 of the Act, by referring the matter to the parties for compromise, or by allowing the petitioner to make instalment payments under section 49 of the Act, or under section 57 of the Act by directing the bank to accept the balance amount from the petitioner. Indeed, the court could have also proceeded under Order XXI, rule 89 the Code by setting aside the sale upon acceptance of 5% interest above the bid money. He also submits that though the bid has been accepted by the court, sale has not yet been confirmed and the bid money not with-drawn by the bank and, as such, the execution proceedings is still pending. Under these circumstances, it is argued, the dispute can still be settled under sections 38 and 45 of the Act or by passing an appropriate order for ends of justice under section 57 of the Act. But the court below without appreciating all these avenues and ignoring the provisions of law most illegally rejected the applications of the petitioner and accepted the bid of the added respondent No.3. In support of his submissions Mr Rahman referred to the judgment of Abdul Momen Bhuiyan and others vs District Judge, Dhaka dated 17-11-2013 passed by the Appellate Division in Civil petition for leave to Appeal No. 2228 of 2011. It suffices to note at this point that the Appellate Division's order as is reproduced later in this judgment is clearly indicative of the need for the Artha Rin Adalat to actively pursue these avenues available under the existing law and, thereby, arrive at a fair and just resolution of the dispute between the parties.

7. Mr Kamruzzaman, learned advocate appearing for the respondent No. 2, in bank opposing the Rule submits that the petitioner has availed of the loan facilities from the bank but failed to repay the loan within time notwithstanding of repeated requests and demands of the bank. The bank tried to sell the mortgaged property through auction under section 12 of the Act but failed as no bidder was found. Thereafter, the bank filed Artha Ain Suit before the Artha Rin Adalat for recovery of the loan against the petitioner. Said Artha Rin Suit was decreed exparte against the petitioner giving him 40 days time to pay the decretal amount but the petitioner failed to pay the money within the said period. Resultantly, the bank filed Artha Jail case and put the decree into execution. The court upon compliance of all relevant provisions of the Act published auction notices in the dailies for sale of the mortgaged property. In the auction three bidders participated and among the bidders the quotation of respondent No. 3 being found highest the court accepted the same with the consent of the bank. There was no illegality in the orders passed by the Adalat. The petitioner got sufficient time to make payment of the decretal amount. But he by filing various applications tried to drag the disposal of the case. It is contended, therefore, that the petitioner in reality is not at all willing to pay the decretal amount. He further submits that the petitioner has no way to get the sale set-aside according to law and prays for discharging the rule.

8. Mr Md Golam Arshad, the learned advocate appearing for the added respondent No. 3 auction purchaser submits that the respondent No. 3 as highest bidder purchased the mortgaged property and paid entire amount of bid money and the court accepted the bid and, as such, he has acquired a right in the property. He further submits that the mortgagor Judgment debtor had two options under rules 89 and 90 of Order XXI of the Code to get the sale set-aside by depositing the decretal amount and 5% above the bid money or by filing an application under rule 90 on the ground of fraud, and illegality, or could claim compensation against the bank. But the petitioner failed to take such steps and, as such, the petitioner has no scope presently to get the sale set-aside. In support of his submissions Mr Arshad referred to the case of M. Karunakara Menon vs M. Krishna Menon reported in 39 ILR (Madras), 429, Banesa Bibi vs Senior Vice President reported in 63 DLR (AD) 160, M/s Antibiotic Stores vs Artha Rin Adalat  reported in 8 MLR (AD) 01 = 55 DLR (AD) 13, M/s Janapriya Rice Mills Ltd. vs Bangladesh reported in 17 BLD 63 = 49 DLR 277, Govt. of Bangladesh vs Sheikh Hasina reported in 16 BLT (AD) 233 and Md Junnur Rahman vs Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha reported in 17 BLD 489 = 50 DLR 39.

9. Heard the learned advocates for the parties, perused the petition, affidavits-in-opposition along with the Annexures appended thereto.

10. Before going through the merit of the rule it would be expedient to look into the relevant provisions of law regarding auction sale and settlement of dispute upon compromise sections 38 and 45 of the Act deal with the settlement of dispute through mediation or corn-promise at any stage of the proceedings and runs thus:

৩৮।(১) এই আইনের অধীন অর্থ ঋণ আদালত মামলায় প্রদত্ত ডিক্রির দারাবাহিকতায় জারী কার্যক্রম অব্যাহত থাকার যে কোন পর্যায় পক্ষগণ মধ্যস্থতার মাধ্যমে জারী মামলার বিষয়বস্তু নিষ্পত্তি করিয়া আদালতকে অবহিত করিতে পারিবে।

(২)উপ-ধারা (১) এর অধীন মধ্যস্থতার ক্ষেত্রে ধারা ২২ এর উপ-ধারা (২)(৩)ও(৪)এ উল্রিথিত বিধান অনুসরণ করিতে হইবে।’

(৩) আদালত উপ-ধারা (১) এর অধীন অবহিত হইলে এবং নিষ্পত্তির বিষয়ে সন্তুষ্ট হইলে উক্ত জারী মোকদ্দমা চুড়ান্তভাবে নিষ্পত্তি করিয়া আদেশ প্রদান করি্বে।

৪৫। (১)(****) এই আইনের কোন কিছুই বিচার কার্যক্রমের পরবর্তী যে কোন পর্যায়ে কোন মামলার আপোষ নিস্পত্তি করা হইতে পক্ষগণকে বারিত করিবে না।

(২) উপ-ধারা (১) এর অধীন প্রদত্ত মামলার আপোষ নিশ্পত্তির সুযোগ এই আইনে মামলা নিস্পত্তির জন্য ব্যবস্তিত অন্যান্য পদ্ধতি এবং নির্ধারিত সময়সীমার হানি বা ব্যত্যয় ঘটাইতে পারিবে না।

11. Both the sections above quoted provide provisions and avenues for the court as well as for the parties to the proceedings to get the dispute settled through mediation and compromise at any stage of the proceedings. In the instant case the execution process is not yet complete. So avenues remain open for the parties to the litigation to get the dispute settled upon taking recourse to the provisions of sections 38 and/or 45 of the Act.

12. Section 49 of the Act deals with the power of the court to allow instalments to the Judgment debtor and runs thus:

৪৯।(১) উপ-ধারা (৩) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে অর্থ ঋণ আদালত বিবাদী-দায়িকের আবেদনের প্রেক্ষিতে বা স্বীয় উদ্যোগে উপযুক্ত মনে করিল ডিক্রিকৃত টাকা ১(এক) বৎসরে ৪(চার) টি সমকিস্তিতে পরিশোধের জন্য দায়িককে সুযোগ প্রদান করিতে পারিবে।

(২)বাদী-ডিক্রিদার সম্মত থাকিলে উপ-ধারা (৩) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, ডিক্রিকৃত টাকা ৩(তিন) বৎসরে ১২(বার)টি সমকিস্তিতে পরিশোধের জন্য আদালত দায়িককে সুযোগ প্রদান করিতে পারিবে।

(৩) উপ-ধারা (১) বা (২) এ উল্লিখিত কোন একটি কিস্তি বকেয়া হওয়া মাত্রই সমুদয় বকেয়া তখনই পরিশোধিতব্য হইবে এবং তদউদ্দেশ্যে জরী কার্যকর যথাবিধি অনুসৃত হইবে।

13. This section authorizes the court to allow the judgment debtor to pay the decretal amount by four instalments within one year or by twelve installments within three years if decree holder gives consent.

14. Section 57 of the Act empowers the court to pass any order for the purposes of securing justice and runs as follows:

৫৭।এই আইনের অধীন অভিপ্রেত ন্যায় বিচারের উদ্দেশ্য সাধনকল্প অথবা আদালতের কার্যক্রমের অপব্যবহার রোধকল্পে প্রযোজনীয় যে কোন পরিপূরক আদেশ প্রদানে আদালতের সহজাত ক্ষমতা কোন কিছু দ্বারা সীমিত করা হইয়াছে বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে না।

15. This section speaks that nothing in the Act shall limit the power of the court in passing any order which, in the opinion of the court, is just and practicable for securing ends of justice.

16. Apart from this, the provisions in Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code in allowing for a sale to be set-aside runs as follows;

17. R 89 Application to set-aside sale on deposit. (1) Where immovable property has been sold in execution of a decree, any person, whose interest has been affected by such sale (provided that such interest has not been voluntarily acquired by him after such sale), may apply to have the sale set-aside on his depositing in Court,

(a) for payment to the purchaser, a sum equal to five percent of the purchase-money, and

(b) for payment to the decree-holder, the amount specified in the proclamation of sale as that for the recovery of which the sale was ordered, less

any amount which may, since the date of such proclamation of sale, have been received by the decree-holder.

18. Said rule 89 of Order gives the judgment debtor an opportunity to get the sale set-aside upon payment of 5% above the bid money and payment of the decretal amount within a specified time. Mr G. Arshad relied upon the judgment in the Karunakara holding that,

"Order XXI, rule 89, Civil Procedure Code, is in the nature of an indulgence to judgment-debtors; and a judgment-debtor who wishes to take advantage of the provisions must strictly comply with the same, by paying all the amounts so directed by the rule, less any amount that may have been paid by himself, and he cannot take credit for any amount paid by a co-judgment-debtor who has not joined him in the application; and according to the rule, credit can be taken only for any amount that may have been actually or constructively received by the decree-holder and not for one which, having been deposited would have been received by him, had he been minded to do so.

19. We are in complete agreement with the above observations regarding the circumstances under which sale may be set-aside by invocation of the process under Order XXI, rule 89.

20. Section 26 of the Act also provides that notwithstanding anything which is not repugnant to the Act relating to the execution of the money decree, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure shall be applicable under the Act. But from the said provision it is obvious that when necessary provisions are already in the Act, the provisions of the Code, would not normally be applicable.

21. Admittedly the execution proceedings is still pending. In view of the provisions contained in sections 38 and 45 of the Act the dispute between the parties can be settled or resolved through mediation and compromise. The petitioner, in fact has taken no step for such mediation and compromise, but filed an application seeking time to pay the bank's dues and for stay of the auction proceedings. Objecting to the perceived dilatory tactic of the petitioner, the Court refused to allow time and/or instalment payments by exercising power under section 49. Therefore, in rejecting the application of the petitioner the Court instead of extending its hand, indeed, narrowed its power in discharging justice.

22. It is also noted that the petitioner filed an application on 16-11-2011 under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code praying for release of the mortgaged property upon payment of 5% interest above the bid money within time as provided by law which was heard on 20-11-2011 and upon hearing the court below vide Order No. 26 of 20-11-2011 rejected the same holding that the petitioner having already filed this writ petition the petition cannot be considered at this stage, the fact of which is reflected in the rule issuing order of this court. This Court is of the view that the court below ought to have disposed of the application on merit in view of the provisions of Order XXI, rules 89 and 92(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, but in not disposing the matter on merit in the light of the provisions of law virtually abdicated its power conferred by law. It is also noted that the petitioner again filed an application on 4-1-2012 for direction upon the bank to accept the balance decretal amount from the petitioner and to set-aside the auction sale upon receipt of 5% interest above the bid money. The court after hearing the said application on 5-1-2012 rejected the same vides its order No. 28 dated 5-1-2012. All these attempts of the petitioner primarily shows his willingness to pay the outstanding dues to the bank.

23. It appears from the available papers in file that the auction was held on 28-9-2011 and accepted on 9-10-2011. The petitioner filed applications praying for time on 26-9-2011, 27-9-2011 and 9-10-2011 to pay the decretal amounts which were rejected by the court. In this regard, the court below could have allowed the application at least under section 57 of the Act as the statutory recognition of its inherent power to do so.

24. Messrs Kamruzzaman and Golam Arshad giving emphasis on section 33 of the Act and Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code argued that the petitioner after holding auction had the option to get the sale set-aside by filing application along with the deposit of 5% interest above the bid money for payment to the auction purchaser and the decretal money for payment to the decree holder but the petitioner has failed to do so and, as such, there is no scope left for the petitioner to get the sale set aside at this stage other than claiming compensation against the bank. But it appears to the Court from the Order Sheets of the court below that the petition repeatedly approached it to allow time at the first instance and urged upon the court to release the property upon depositing 5% interest above the bid money and sought a direction upon the bank to accept the balance decretal money at the latest. All those efforts of the petitioner prove to be futile. Had it been considered by the Court at the 1st instance the matter would have been settled long ago.

25. From the papers available on record, it appears that the sale is yet to be confirmed as contemplated in rule 92 (1) of the Order XXI of the Code. Admittedly, in the instant case the sale has hot yet been confirmed. Nor has it become absolute as no formal order of confirmation of sale has been passed by the court below. In paragraph 2 of his supplementary affidavit, the petitioner has stated that he already paid Taka 1,15,000 to the bank out of the decretal amount of Taka 4,60,735. It is evident furthermore that the auction purchaser added respondent on 3 deposited the balance auction money amounting to Taka 5,10,000 on 16-10-2011.

26. Mr. Rahman the learned advocate for the petitioner further submits that in a similar situation our Appellate Division passed a judgment in CPLA No. 7778 of 2011 in the case of Abdul Momen Bhuiyan vs District Judge, Dhaka & others wherein it has been held that:

"In several cases including the cases of Ganyson Ltd. and another vs Sonali Bank and other, (1985) 37 DLR (AD) 42 and AFM Naziruddin vs Mrs Hameeda Banu (1993) 45 DLR (AD) 38, this Division previously exercised the power of doing complete jus-tice under Article 104 of the constitution. The subject matter of the instant case represents on occasion to and demands exercise of this by this Division for the purpose of protection of the dwelling house of the petitioners The petitioners stated to have paid the entire dues payable to the HBFC. Admittedly, the auction purchaser, respondent No. 3 deposited 75,25,000 on 22-6-2010 and he should be compensated by the petitioners to retain their valuable house situated at Mirpur, Dhaka. Therefore, the petitioners are directed to pay Taka 12,00,000 (twelve lakh) to the auction purchaser (respondent no. 3) as compensation within 45 days ".

<u>27. Under our constitutional scheme, this court has no scope to do complete justice as does the Appellate Division. But this court finds that section 57 of the Act, empowers the Artha Rin Adalat to give adequate relief in cases as in hand, even if it is assumed but not conceded that there is no scope to give the petitioner appropriate relief by the Artha Rin Adalat under the other provision of the Act. Furthermore, in view of the facts and circumstance of this case, the High Court Division is competent enough to give such relief in exercise of its powers under Article 102 of the Constitution as is necessary to safeguard the petitioner's fundamental right to property under Article 42 of the constitution.</u>

28. It is also noted that the impugned orders passed by the court are interlocutory and not final orders and thus no appeal/revision can be taken therefrom as per provision of section 44(2) of the Act and, therefore, the present writ is maintainable.

29. Given the facts and circumstances of the present case, since the auction has not yet been confirmed by the executing court and since the mortgaged property is the only home-stead of the petitioner as claimed by the petitioner, for protecting the homestead of the petitioner in our considered view, it was a fit case to exercise the powers under section 57 of the Ain to give adequate relief to the petitioner, but which the Artha Rin Adalat failed to exercise under said section. In these circumstances we are inclined to dispose of this Rule with the direction to the petitioner judgment debtor to pay 10% above the bid money to the auction purchaser and the balance decretal amount along with the other costs to the bank decree holder within 30 days of the receipt of the certified copy of this judgment and order, failing which the auction sale shall stand absolute.

<u>30. Before parting with, this court observes that since the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 is a special law and some latitude is being given to the judgment debtor to get the dispute settled through mediation or compromise and an extensive power has been given to the court to secure justice under sections 38,45,49 and 57 of the Act, the Artha Rin Adalat ought to have acted following the provisions contained in law as observed above by this court in supersession of the other provisions contained in any other law as per section 3 of the Act. But to our utter surprise we see that the Artha Rin Adalat almost in every case is reluctant to extend its hands to help the litigants taking recourse to the above mentioned sections of the Ain making them virtually ineffective.</u>

31. It is also noted that the intention of the legislature is to recover money not to sell or own the property of the mortgagor making them homeless. Keeping in mind the intention of legislature the Artha Rin Adalat can pass any order for the purpose of securing justice considering facts and circumstances of each individual case.

32. With the above observations and directions the rule is disposed of however without any order as to costs.

33. Order of stay granted at the time of issuance of rule is hereby recalled and stand vacated.

34. Communicate a copy of the judgment to the court concerned.

Syed Refaat Ahmed J: Concurring as I do with the findings and observations of Mahmudul Hoque, J. above, I feel nevertheless the necessity to emphasize the point made by him as to the need to apply the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 ("Act") in light of its true ambit and purport. This necessarily entails a balancing of all Acts provisions applicable in each given case and aiming at achieving the best possible practicable solution for the ends of justice. In that regard, it is this Court's view that the statutorily designated court, i.e. the Artha Rin Adalat consistently appears to shy away from giving a beneficial interpretation to the Act. Thereby, precious opportunities are readily passed over under the Act to mitigate that statute's obvious harshness as operates against judgment-debtors. This stems, this Court finds, from an ingrained inability to appreciate that the core objective of the Act at debt recovery must not invariably without further qualification entail the acquisition of a defaulter/judgment-debtor's property. On the contrary there is nothing in the Act that dictates the inevitability of such consequence. Rather, the Act aims expressly to achieve the opposite. Provisions, most notably, in sections 22, 38, 45, 49 and 57, emphatically attest to that statutory intent. But undue conservatism per se or misconceived reservations either to explore avenues of equitable alternative amicable settlement processes endorsed by the Act itself or to exercise its inherent jurisdiction, for reasons not entirely evident to this Court, operate regrettably to bind the Adalat's hand as it were. In that con-text, the Adalat has instead grown so complacently used to a selective and preferential reliance of certain provisions of the Act, that the said Act, particularly through over-subscription to the provisions of section 33(5) and (7), is inappropriately seen as pandering to the acquisitive tendencies of decree-holder banks and financial institutions rather than to facilitating the full recovery of their loans. There is seen, therefore, a failure by the Adalat to strike an essential balance between financial interests of financial institutions and the fundamental proprietary interests of judgment- debtors that clearly is the Act's objective and purpose. Such abdication of statutory authority and jurisdiction by the Adalat as a matter of course has led to the above-referred provisions being relegated by disuse to the unavoidable status as dead letters of the law in stark discordance with clear legislative intent to the contrary. This Court is of the view, therefore, that such a situation needs to be addressed and redressed urgently. It is with that intent that this judgment and Order is particularly being communicated to the concerned Artha Rin Adalat.

End.

lawyer:
Tanjibul Alam, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
M Hafizullah, Senior Advocate with Md Al-Amin Sarker and Md Ohiullah—For Respondent No. 1. 
Naima Haider, Deputy Attorney-General with Md Imam Hossain, Assistant Attorney-General-For the Proforma Respondent.

full_judgment:
This is an Application under section 7Ka of the Arbitration Act, 2001 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") for the preservation and protection of the subject-matter of the dispute arising out of import of a consignment of sugar ("the goods") entered into between the petitioner and the respondent.

2. It is stated in the Application that in accordance with the terms of a contractual arrangement the respondent being required to ship all the goods by the end of November, 2006 could do so only with regard to a partial consignment of the goods while the remaining goods were shipped beyond the contractual period. It is also stated that the petitioner having consequentially sought to resolve that dispute by invoking the arbitration provisions evident in such contractual arrangement served a notice upon the respondent on 27-3-2007 claiming a payment of US $ 194,400 by way of damages arising by reason of the respondent's breach of contract (Annexure-'E'). This Application was also filed against the backdrop of the goods having nevertheless arrived at Chittagong with the petitioner apprehending the imminent sale by auction of the same by the pro-forma respondent Commissioner of Customs. In these circumstances the prayer made was for issuing a notice upon the respondent to show cause as to why the goods imported under Letter of Credit No. 087906010304 dated 23-9-2006 then lying with the Commissioner of Customs shall not be attached in favour of the petitioner and why an order of injunction should not be issued restraining the Commissioner of Customs from auctioning the goods till disposal of this Application. Pursuant further to another prayer for an ad interim injunction restraining the respondent and the Commissioner of Customs from taking any steps towards the release or auction of the goods, this Court in addition to issuing a notice to show cause upon the respondent on 25-4-2007 ordered the goods to be attached by way of an ad interim order directing further the Commissioner of Customs to inform this Court prior to taking any steps in respect of the goods.

3. The Application identifies a document dated 12-9-2006 bearing Reference No.6 /S/ 47071 for the supply of 2,700 metric tonnes of the goods as the contract" in this case (Annexure-'A'). It is stated that it is consequent to this "contract" that the above-referred Letter of Credit No. 087906010304 dated 23-9-2006 was opened in favour of the respondent (Annexure-'B'). The dispute between the petitioner and the respondent has its genesis from the fact of the respondent denying and disputing the very existence of the contract dated 12-9-2006. The position, therefore, necessarily adopted by the respondent is that since there was no contract of the supply of the goods in question as otherwise identified by petitioner as being the document dated 12-9-2006 (Annexure-A) and since, consequentially, the arbitration clause evident in that document is also ostensibly not in evidence of any agreement between the petitioner and the respondent, this Application is not maintainable and is liable to be rejected by reason of it been shorn of its raison deter. Consequentially, the respondent also prays for the order of attachment dated 25-4-2007 to be vacated. Relying upon documents brought on record by itself, the respondent insists upon the businesses relationship between the petitioner and the respondent being instead first initiated through a Proforma Invoice dated 13-9-2006 bearing, however, the same reference number as the document in Annexure-'A' dated 12-9-2006, i.e., 6/S/47071. Reading the Proforma Invoice coupled with the relevant provision of the Letter of Credit and amendments subsequently introduced into the Letter of Credit affecting the shipment period, it is the respondent's contention that all consignments were duly shipped within time but the petitioner and its Bank having since refused to make payment for the goods constituting the second consignment and having, thereby, refused to receive the same, are in effect trying to secure the deli-very of the goods to be made in favour of the petitioner without making any payment and, thereby, causing the petitioner to benefit from an illegal gain. Against this backdrop, the respondent adopts the position that the entire scheme is one of the petitioner attempting at defrauding the supplier respondent and that in this regard the petitioner has, in particular, used the Order of Attachment of 25-4-2007 to its benefit.

4. From the factual matrices above, it is evident that two hurdles have been placed by the respondent before the petitioner. The first has to do with the extent to which, if at all, the document dated 12-9-2006 prevails along with the particular arbitration clause specified therein over and above the Proforma Invoice of 13-9-2006 in governing the contractual relationship between the two parties. The second has to do with the right, if at all, of the petitioner to seek an attachment of the goods, given that the petitioner has not paid for the same by means of retiring the necessary and relevant bills of lading. In the latter case, the respondent has further expressed concern at the petitioner's application before this Court for the disposal of the attached goods by sale in the local market arranged by the petitioner itself and placing the proceeds of such sale in "Suspense Account/Escrow Account". Explaining the apprehension that with the passage of time the goods, which are of perishable nature, would become unfit for human consumption and, consequentially, emerge as a total loss to the petitioner itself, the petitioner in filing the application for a disposal of the goods also submitted that such sale at its behest would not adversely affect the Government, in particular. In opposing that application the respondent has been at pains to highlight the fact that the petitioner having not paid the price of the goods to the L/C opening bank, which in turn not having made payment to the beneficiary bank, and the shipping documents having not been negotiated, the question of the petitioner undertaking a sale of the goods in open market without proper title to the same does not arise. As a corollary to that, the respondent has asserted its status as an unpaid vendor entitled to get the goods re-exported out of Bangladesh. The other angle to the issue of attachment is introduced by the respondent itself in its Affidavit-in-Opposition submitting that because of long storage of the goods under the control and possession of the Commissioner of Customs, the respondent has already been saddled with a huge liability in respect of varied costs, taxes, duties as are mounting up by the day. It is stated in the Affidavit-in-Opposition and that it is against that backdrop that the Commissioner of Customs took steps for the auction sale of the goods but was deterred doing so because of this Court's Order of attachment dated 25-4-2007. In this regard, it is noted that the Proforma-respondent Commissioner of Customs, upon invoking the authority under section 82 of the Customs Act, 1969 did, in fact, issue a notice dated 10-4-2007 to auction the goods, contingent upon the petitioner addressee/ recipient of that notice failing to secure the release of the goods within the period specified therein (Annexure-'F' to the Application).

5. The stance adopted by the Commissioner of Customs vis-a-vis the goods is further amply made clear in an Affidavit-in-Opposition filed on behalf of the Commissioner of Customs praying that this Court may vacate the Order of attachment dated 25-4-2007, thereby, allowing the Commissioner of Customs to hold that auction as early as possible failing which irreparable loss would be caused to the said Proforma respondent. The actual quantum of that loss in terms of duty and charges remaining unpaid thus far has been specified as standing at Taka 43,85,885.50 in Supplementary Affidavit filed before this Court on behalf of the Commissioner of Customs. It is against this factual and contractual milieu that this Court is now asked to grant the necessary interim measures of protection under section 7Ka of the Act.

6. Heard the learned Advocates for the petitioner and the respondent, and the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the Proforma-respondent and perused the various Application Affidavit and all documents brought on record by the parties.

<u>7. It is evident to this Court that bearing in mind the specific provisions of section 7 of the Act read with the rather exceptional provisions of section 7Ka this Court has been asked at the outset to determine the very existence of the arbitration agreement pursuant to which the notice dated 27-3-2007 was served upon the respondent (Annexure-'E'). In this regard, it is submitted that the measures as may be granted and adopted shall be in aid of the consequential arbitral proceedings in a manner that the decision of the Arbitral Tribunal and the award that it may make does not at the end of the day appear to be hollow. In other words, the purpose of any section 7Ka application is for the protection and preservation of the subject-matter of arbitral proceedings with a view to ensuring that any future award may remain effectively executable. For this Court to exercise its discretion under section 7Ka of the Act it is, in the view of this Court, sine qua non that there be a prima facie satisfaction that there has indeed, at one point in time or other been a meeting of minds between the parties to this Application to refer their disputes within a certain contractual selling to arbitration. The learned Advocate for the respondent Mr Md Ohiullah has vigorously argued by a reference to various precedents: 1996 2(SC) pages 667; AIR 1987 (SC) 1918; AIR 2000 (SC) 1379 and 1993 1 (SC) 230), that it would indeed, by various precedents be within the power and authority of this Court to determine the existence of an arbitration agreement. That notwithstanding, this Court is also mindful of the fact of the need to strike an essential balance between granting interim measures and the prudence in not encroaching upon any Arbitral Tribunal's ultimate authority to decide upon the existence, nature and scope of such arbitration agreement. Proceeding upon that cautionary note and examining in particular the document dated 12-9-2006 identified as "the contract" by the petitioner (Annexure-'A'), the Proforma Invoice of the following date relied upon and identified by the respondent to be the sole documentary evidence in support of any contractual arrangement between the parties, and the Letter of Credit and the amendments thereto as followed subsequently, it is this Court's view that these documents taken together establish a prima facie pattern of performance negotiation and course of conduct by the parties in this Application. The sequence with which the Proforma Invoice dated 13-9-2006 follows the document dated 12-9-2006 and identified by the petitioners as "the contract" within a span of 24 hours, the fact of such Proforma Invoice bearing the same reference number as that found on "the contract" itself i.e., 06/S/47071 and the fact of the unit price of US$ 387 per MT of the goods identified in the Proforma Invoice which can only properly be understood by reference to the explanation provided in the earlier document dated 12-9-2006 as being the price fixed net of the deposit already paid in advance by the petitioner for the goods otherwise regularly priced at US$ 407 per MT, have satisfied this Court that the contractual arrangement between the parties is one of a composite nature with "the contract" dated 12-9-2006 and the Proforma Invoice dated 13-9-2006 being the essential components thereof. The reference number found to be common to both these documents also, in the view of this Court, gives rise to a presumption of a contractual arrangement arrived at by means of necessary incorporation by reference whereby the arbitration clause found in the document dated 12-9-2006 may be read as being incorporated in the Proforma Invoice itself. The said arbitration clause reads thus:</u>

<u>"Arbitration</u>

<u>All disputes arising out of or in conjunction with this Contract shall be refer-red to The Refined Sugar Association for settlement in accordance with the rules relating to arbitration. The contract shall be governed by and construed in accordance with English Law."</u>

<u>Indeed, a perusal of these documents though revealing a certain sequence of contractual conduct and performance by the parties, also raises complex and problematic questions of offer, counter-offer and the like as well and must have a bearing on one or the other parties' contention as what construed the agreed upon valid period shipment under the contract. That question, and bearing in mind the issue of striking the essential balance as observed hereinbefore, must be one for the relevant Arbitral Tribunal to deliberate and decide upon.</u>

8. The second aspect of this Application is to the justifiability of not only the attachment and restraint Orders prayed for must necessarily be addressed, however, in the facts and circumstances of this case by first addressing the issue of the ad interim Order of attachment made on 25-4-2007. Upon a consideration of the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr M Hafizullah this Court by reference also to the cases reported in 1993 BLD (AD) 211, 7 BLT (AD) 381 is of the view that the petitioner cannot validly lay claim to any title in the goods. The problem for the petitioner in this regard is compounded by several other factors. Given this Court's finding that the petitioner did not have any title to the goods on any material date having admittedly not paid for the same and not returned the relevant bills of lading, in that regard, the post-attachment Order application filed by the petitioner for a disposal of the goods by a self-arranged sale in the local open market appears to be misconceived at the very least. In making that application the petitioner appears to have overlooked the legal consequences of the fact of the present control over the goods being physically exercised by the Proforma respondent Commissioner of Customs who with the passage of time, and in the circumstances of the petitioner having admittedly failed to take the delivery of the goods within the defined statutory period, has invoked the authority under section 82 of the Customs Act for a sale of the goods by auction. In that regard, this Court is in agreement with the submissions of the learned Deputy Attorney-General Ms Naima Haider that the fact of the Commissioner of Customs having the statutory lien over the goods was overlooked by the petitioner in making that particular application. Ms Haider has also submitted that in order to see to the effective exercise of the Commissioner's statutory authority under section 82 it would now be proper for this Court to vacate the order of attachment and allow for the statutory process to take its due course. Ms Haider has also thrown light by referring to Lawrence Loat Ltd vs Ajay Incorporated & Siltrate International Ltd reported in 1997 BLD 159 = 2 BLC 327 that an order of attachment before judgment may be secured under Order XXXVIII, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure upon a concrete allegation substantiated by sufficient material to the satisfaction of the Court that the respondent has been doing an act for removing the goods from the jurisdiction of this Court with the intention of delaying or obstructing the due process of this Court. Applying that test, this Court finds no more than a general allegation made by the petitioner of the imminent repatriation of the goods from Bangladesh ostensibly with a view to defeat the claim of the petitioner Stray references to a statement made on record by the respondent as to its willingness to re-export the goods are not found to be further substantiated by the petitioner either by submission made or documentary evidence produced to impute any ill-intention on the part of the respondent in this regard on the material dates. Further, in this regard this Court has taken note of Mr Md Ohiullah's submissions at length bearing on the fact that prior to the notice of arbitration served on 27-3-2007 and the Arbitration Application proceedings being commenced in this Court on 25-4-2007 there was, in fact, no embargo on the respondent to seek to take back its cargo as an unpaid vendor, such efforts being evident in the respondent's communication, back and forth, with the concerned bank and the Commissioner of Customs at a point in time when it had no notice had dispute having arisen Court's satisfaction as to effective steps being taken to consume arbitration. These factors now collectively contribute to this Court's view that the Order of attachment and the order of restraint evident in the Order dated 25-4-2007 must now necessarily be vacated. That being the case and given that the Commissioner of Customs by virtue of section 82 of the Customs Act is now entitled to sell the goods in auction, the goods, and as more fully described in the Schedule to the Application thus:

i. Consignment of 215 MT (4300 bags) of sugar imported under Bill of Lading No. EISU 360600098314 dated 11-12-2006 bearing Import Rotation No. 47/07 and L /No. 05 = 10' x 20' FCL Cont;

ii. Consignment of 540 MT (10,800 bags) of sugar imported under Bill of Lading No. MOLU-781404693 dated 5-12-2006 bearing Import Rotation No. 02/07 and L/No. S/Cont/mol-06 = 20' x 20' FCL Cont;

iii. Consignment of 540 MT (10,800 bags) of sugar imported under Bill of Lading No. HJSCSSZA 00612906 bearing Import Rotation No. 213/07 and L /No. RSL-17 = 5' x 20' FCL Cont,

are now, hereby directed and ordered by this Court to be sold by the Proforma Respondent Commissioner of Customs in exercise of his authority under section 82 of the Customs Act,1969 as soon as possible. It would also be for this Court to ensure that the procedure for sale and the application of the sale proceeds conform to the provisions of section 201 of the Customs Act. Section 201 reads thus:

"201. Procedure for sale of goods and application of sale proceeds—(1) Where any goods, other than confiscated goods, are to be sold under any provision of this Act, they shall be sold, after due notice to the owner, by public auction or by tender or by private offer or, with the consent of the owner in writing, in any other manner.

(2) The sale proceeds shall be applied to the following purposes in their respective order, namely

(a)	first to pay the expenses of the sale;

(b) then to pay the freight or other charges, if any, payable in respect of the goods, if notice of such charges has been given to the person holding the goods in custody;

(c) then to pay the customs duty, other taxes and dues payable to the [Government] in respect of such goods:

(d) then to pay the charges due to the person holding such goods in custody;

(3) The balance, if any, shall be paid to the owner of the goods, provided he applies for it within six months of the sale of the goods or shows sufficient cause for not doing so."

Given the calculation sheet produced by the Commissioner of Customs it would now be in place that pursuant to the sale of the goods in public auction as prayed for by the Commissioner of Customs, the sale proceeds shall be applied for the following specific purposes and in their respective order as directed here under:

A. First, towards defraying the sale expenses;

B. Second, towards payment covering the amount of Taka 39,80,737.50 (Taka Thirty-nine Lac, Eighty Thousand, Seven Hundred and Thirty-seven and Fifty Paisa) only as claimed by the Commissioner of Customs to cover customs duty, assessable and payable on the goods. The additionally claimed amount of Taka 4,05,148 (Taka Four Lac, Five Thousand, One Hundred and Forty-eight) only by way of Advance Trade VAT (ATV) may also be recoverable from the sale proceeds by the Commissioner of Customs from any persons or entity appropriately and duly liable to be assessed for and to pay the same under the law;

C. Third, towards payment(s) of all charges due to any person or entity , including but not limited to The Chittagong, Port Authority, and incurred on account of the holding of the goods in custody;

D. The balance, if any, of such sale proceeds shall be handed over by the Commissioner of Customs, through the agency of the Office of the Attorney-General, positively within 3 (three) months from the date of the sale of the goods to the Registrar, Supreme Court of Bangladesh for the purpose of being deposited and maintained in the Registrar's Account subject to further orders from this Court and pending the outcome of the Arbitral Proceedings and the award made, if any, by the Arbitral Tribunal.

9. In the light of the above, this Court is now inclined to dispose of this Application with the observations and directions made above.

There is no order as to costs.

End.
