case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 46-2000 passed by the High Division in PMA No.95 of 1990)
full_judgment:
Md Muzammel Hossain J: This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 4-6-2000 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in PMA No. 95 of 1990 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and order dated 21-10-1989 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (presently Joint District Judge), Commercial Court No. 2, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 20 of 1986 dismissing the same. 
2. The appellant as petitioner instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 124 of 1984 which was subsequently renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 20 of 1986 before the learned Subordinate Judge, Commercial Court No. 2, Dhaka for realization of a sum of Taka 63,54,326.33 as on 1-1-1984 under Article 33 of the President's Order No. 128 of 1972 from the opposite parties-respondents stating, interalia, that the petitioner-appellant Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha (hereinafter referred to as BSRS) was established by PO No.128 of 1972 to provide credit facilities and other assistance to industrial concerns and to broaden the base of investment in Bangladesh. On the application of the respondent No. 1 the appellant-BSRS sanctioned a loan of Taka 70,00,000 on 18-12-1979 for acquisition of two steel body self propelled Cargo Coasters of 600 DWT each. The loan is repayable in sixteen equal half-yearly installments commencing from two years after disbursement of the first installment which was disbursed on 30-12-1980. To that effect a loan agreement was entered into on 6-6-1980 between the respondent No. 1. She Shipping Lines Limited and the appellant-BSRS. Thereafter a tripartite contract was executed on 29-11-1980 between the appellant BSRS, the respondent No.1-She Shipping Lines Limited and the respondent No. 5 Rajdhani Ship Building and Engineering Works Ltd to build the body of two vessels in the dockyard and a total amount of Taka 42 lakhs was disbursed in two installments. The first installment of Taka 14 lakhs was disbursed for building the body of the vessels and the last installment of Taka 28 lakhs was meant for opening of L/C to import engines for the vessels. The total amount of Taka 42 lakhs was disbursed by cheque to the account of the respondent No. 5. But the respondent No. 5 did not import the new marine engines as per terms of the contract rather they imported reconditioned engines which are now lying in the godown of the Rupali Bank and misappropriated the money. Thirty five percent of the construction of the body of the vessel had been completed on 14-3-1983. Since then no progress had been made though the date of delivery of the vessels as per agreement dated 31-10-1983. The appellant claims that the respondent Nos. 1-4 being guarantors are jointly and severally liable to repay the BSRS's dues. 
3. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 contested the case by filing written objection denying all the material allegations stating, interalia, that the appellant sanctioned an amount of Taka 70 lakh on 18-12-1979 to purchase two steel body self-propelled Coasters of 600 DWT each and the loan was repayable by 16 half yearly installments commencing from 2 years after disbursement of the loan; that a tripartite contract was entered into among the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha, the appellant, Rajdhani Ship Building Engineering Works Ltd and She Shipping Lines Ltd, the respondents; that under the tripartite contract the installment was required to be paid to the respondent No. 5 directly; that as per terms and conditions of the contract Bank to Bank L/C was to be opened. But in fact, it was not followed and consequently, the officials of the appellant and the respondent No. 5 took advantage of it and misappropriated the whole money; that the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 are not responsible for payment of loan money. 
4. The learned Subordinate Judge, Commercial Court No. 2, Dhaka found the appellant and the respondent No. 5 solely liable for breach of contract and frustration of the project and by the judgment and order dated 21-10-1989 dismissed the miscellaneous case on contest against the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and ex-parte against the rest without cost. The appellant being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order dated 21-10-1989 preferred First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 95 of 1990 before the High Court Division which was pleased to dismiss the same by the judgment and order dated 4-6-2000. 
5. The petitioner-appellant being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order dated 4-6-2000 passed by the High Court Division preferred the instant Appeal with the leave of this Court. Leave was granted to consider the following grounds: 
(I) whether the respondent No. 1-She Shipping Lines Limited is a loanee at law, because of (1) the loan agreement entered into between the petitioner and the respondent No. 1 on 6-6-1986, (2) the tripartite contract executed on 29-11-1980 by the petitioner-BSRS, respondent No. 1-She Shipping Lines Limited and the respondent No. 5-builder, Rajdhani Ship Building and Engineering Works Limited, (3) the personal guarantees and Demand, Promissory Notes etc. executed by its directors for Taka 42,00,000 which was received by the respondent No. 5-Rajdhani Ship Building and Engineering Works Limited, (4) the withdrawal and misappropriation of Taka 42 lakh by the respondent Nos.6 and 7, the Managing Director and the Director respectively of the respondent No. 5 as agents from it's account (5) the importation of second hand engines in place of brand new engines. Whether all these make the respondent No. 1 and other respondents personally liable for wrong doing, misfeasance, malfeasance and breach of trust and, as such, they are liable for payment of BSRS dues. 
(II) whether both the trial court and the High Court Division committed error of law and facts by holding that the respondent Nos.l and 2 knew only of the disbursement of the first installment, although by Exhibit 19 the respondent No. 1 She Shipping Lines Limited had requested BSRS, the petitioner to disburse second installment for procurement of engines and, as such, the judgment of the trial Court and the High Court Division are not sustainable in law and in facts. 
6. Mr AKM Nazrul Islam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the appellant submits that the respondent No. 1, being a loanee at law, under the terms and conditions of the loan agreement, entered into between the appellant and the respondent No. 1 on 6-6-1980 and the tripartite contract executed on 29-11-1980 by the appellant-BSRS, the respondent No. 1 She Shipping Lines Ltd and the respondent No. 5 builder Rajdhani Ship Building and Engineering Works Ltd, the personal guarantees and Demand, Promissory Notes etc. executed by the Directors of She Shipping Lines Ltd for Taka 42,00,000 which was received by the respondent No. 5-Rajdhani Ship Building & Engineering Works Ltd, the withdrawal and misappropriation of Taka 42 lakh by the respondent Nos.6 and 7 from the account of the respondent No. 5 was done as agents and the importation of second-hand engine in place of brand new engine in the name of Rajdhani Ship Building and Engineering Works Ltd having done by the directors of Rajdhani Ship Building and Engineering Works Ltd who are personally liable for their wrong doing, misfeasance, malfeasance and breach of trust and, as such, all the respondents are liable for payment of BSRS dues. Mr Nazrul Islam then submits that both the trial Court and the High Court Division were wrong in holding that the respondent Nos.l and 2 knew only of the disbursement of the first installment, although by exhibit 19 the respondent No.  1, She Shipping Lines Ltd had requested the appellant, BSRS to disburse second installment for procurement of engines and that both the trial Court and the High Court Division committed error of law and facts and, as such, the judgments of the trial Court and the High Court Division are not sustainable in law and in facts. The learned Advocate appearing for the appellant further submits that both the Courts were wrong in not holding that collusion existed between the respondent No. 1 and the respondent No. 5 and not between the appellant and the respondent No. 5. Finally, he submits that the trial Court and the High Court Division were wrong in not holding that by non-completing the project the She Shipping Lines Ltd and the Rajdhani Ship Building and Engineering Works Ltd have committed breach of contract violating the provisions of loan agreement and the tripartite contract under which they are bound to complete the Project and, as such, the appeal is liable to be allowed. 
7. Mr Md Aftab Hossain, the learned Advocate-on-Record appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 2 submits that both the trial Court and the High Court Division concurrently found that the appellant and the respondent No. 5 in collusion with each other violated the tripartite contract and, as such, the respondent No. 2 is not liable for money claimed by the appellant. He then submits that the trial Court and the High Court Division have rightly held that the respondent No. 2 had no knowledge about payment to the respondent No. 5 by the appellant and, as such, both the respondent Nos.l and 2 are exempted from any liability of the appellant. Mr Aftab Hossain contends that both the trial Court and the High Court Division have rightly held that collusion existed between the appellant and the respondent No.  5 and the respondent No. 2 has nothing to do in respect of loan money of the appellant. The learned Advocate-on-record appearing for the respondent No.  2 finally submits that the trial Court and the High Court Division have rightly held that the respondent No. 2 is in no way liable for the loan money, on the other hand, the respondent No. 2 has been seriously affected for not completing the project by the respondent No. 5 and, as such, the appeal is liable to be dismissed. 
8. We have heard the learned Advocates for both the parties, perused the leave granting order, impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, Concise Statements filed by the parties and other materials on record. 
9. In the instant case Md Junnur Rahman, Senior Principal Officer of BSRS as PW 1 in examination-in-chief stated that on 18-12-1979 the appellant-BSRS sanctioned a loan of Taka 70,00,000 (seventy lakh) for two steel body self-propelled Coasters of 600 DWT each and the loan was repayable by 16 half-yearly installments commencing from 2 years after disbursment of the first installment and accordingly, an agreement for loan was signed on 6-6-1980 with the respondent No. 1. The first installment was disbursed on 30-12-1980. Previously on 28-12-1980, the respondent No. 1 requested the appellant to make payment of the first installment in favour of the respondent No. 5 by letter dated 24-12-1980 which was proved and marked as Exhibit 12 and accordingly, first installment amounting to Taka 14,00,000 (fourteen lakh) was paid to the respondent No. 5. At the request of the respondent Nos.1 and 5, the appellant disbursed the money of second installment amounting to Taka 28,00,000 on 20-1-1981 with an advice to the Rupali Bank under Wage Earner's Scheme A/C Rajdhani Ship Building and Engineering Works Ltd and according to that advice two new engines as per Proforma Invoice were required to be imported through Rupali Bank. The respondent Nos. 5-7 violating the terms and conditions of the tripartite agreement imported two old engines. When they were asked about it they stated that on request of the respondent No. 1 they had imported these old engines. The respondent No. 1 by it's letter dated 28-8-1982 (Exhibit 17) gave their consent in the importation of old engines. PWI further deposed that the respondents collusively imported old engines instead of new engines. In cross-examination PW 1 stated that the respondent No. 1, sponsor and the respondent No.  5, builder violated the terms and conditions of the tripartite contract inasmuch as the respondent No. 5 violated the terms and condition of the contract by importing old engines and the respondent No. 1 violated the terms and conditions of the contract by giving it's consent to their act. PW 1 in cross-examination also stated that the appellant did not pay any money to the sponsor, respondent No. 1 because it was stipulated in the tripartite contract that money would be disbursed in favour of the respondent No, 5. Accordingly, the appellant paid money to the respondent No. 5. Initially Taka 14,00,000 (fourteen lakh) was paid. PW 1 in cross-examination further stated that at the time of payment of second installment amounting to Taka 28,00,000 (twenty eight lakh) they advised for opening of bank to bank LC but the sponsor, respondent No.  1 did not pay any heed to it. This advice was proved and marked as Exhibit 15. The cheque was sent with the advise letter. There was no LC number in the advise. PW 1 in cross-examination also stated that the respondent No. 1 in collusion with the respondent No. 5, builder encashed payment of second installment. PW 1 in cross-examination stated that after importation of the engines they came to know that these were second-hand engines and then they called explanation from the respondent No. 5 and in reply, the respondent No. 5 stated that with the advice of the respondent No. 1 sponsor they imported the engines. It appears that the engines were not imported as per specification. The respondent Nos. 1 and 5 in collusion with each other imported the old engines and thereby they violated the terms and conditions of the contract. The respondent No. 1 on 14-12-1982 gave an undertaking (Exhibit 18), stating, that in association with the respondent No. 5-builder, they imported old engines for which they are fully responsible. The respondent No. 1 by its letter dated 6-1-1981 requested the appellant to make payment against second installment whereupon they paid the second installment to the respondent No.  5. The letter of request issued by the respondent No. 1 was proved and marked as Exhibit 19. The appellant performed its part of the contract but the respondent Nos. 1 and 5 failed to perform their part of the contract. 
10. Mazharul Huq Majumder, PW 2, Senior Principal Officer of the Accounts Department of the appellant Bank formally proved the Statement of Accounts which was marked as Exhibit 20. AM Serajul Karim, the Company Manager of the respondent No. 1-company as DW 1 in examination-in-chief stated that there was a tripartite contract executed by the appellant-BSRS, the respondent No.  1 sponsor and the respondent No. 5 builder. As per terms and conditions of the contract the appellant was required to make the payment of loan in favour of the builder-respondent No. 5. DWI denied that they in collusion with the respondent No. 5-builder had imported old engines to misappropriate the payment of second installment. 
11. In the instant case, it appears that the appellant BSRS sanctioned a loan of Taka 70 lakh in favour of the respondent No.  1, borrower, for construction of two steel body self-propelled coasters of 600 DWT each and the loan was repayable by 16 half-yearly installments commencing from two years after disbursement of the first installment as per loan agreement dated 6-6-1980. The first installment of Taka 14 lakh was disbursed on 30-12-1980 to the respondent No. 5 as per instruction of the respondent No. 1 vide letter dated 24-12-1980 (Exhibit 12) and thereafter as per request of respondent Nos. 1 and 5, the appellant disbursed the 2nd installment amounting to Taka 28 lath on 20-1-1981 with an advice (Exhibit 15) to the account of Rajdhani Ship Building and Engineering Works Ltd with Rupali Bank endorsing copies of the same to the respondent Nos.l and 5 to import new Caterpillar 3412 Marine Propulsion Engines as per proforma invoice and in the said advice the appellant categorically stated that the amount would be utilized for the aforesaid purpose. There was a tri-partite contract dated 29-11-1980 (Exhibit 10) among the appellant-BSRS, the respondent No.  1-borrower-purchaser and the respondent No. 5-builder to build and deliver to the respondent No.  1-purchaser two new steel body self-propelled cargo coasters/vessels in the dock-yard. On perusal of memo dated 6-1-1981 (Exhibit 19) it appears that the respondent No. 1 requested the appellant to disburse second installment to the respondent No.  5 for procurement of engines as per appellant's letter to the latter. At the time of disbursement of second installment of Taka 28 lakh the appellant vide Memo No. E1152 dated 20-1-1981 (Exhibit 15) advised to open letter of credit for importing new caterpillar 3412 Marine Propulsion engines but the respondent No. 1 did not pay any heed to it. The respondent No. 5 in collusion with the respondent No. 1 encashed the payment of second installment in their personal name in violation of the terms and conditions contained in the loan agreement dated 6-5-1980 (Exhibit I) and imported two second-hand reconditioned marine engines. When appellant came to know about the second-hand reconditioned engines it called explanation from respondent No. 5 who in reply stated that they had imported the secondhand reconditioned engines with the advice of respondent No. 1. Thereby the respondent No. 1 violated the terms and conditions of the contract. Admittedly, the engines were not imported as per stipulation of the contract. On perusal of respondent No. 1's letter dated 28-8-1982 (Exhibit 17) addressed to the respondent No. 5, it appears that the respondent No. 1 approved the supply of the second-hand reconditioned engines by respondent No. 5. Thereafter, the respondent No. 1 admitted that they had violated the terms and conditions of the contract and gave an undertaking dated 14-12-1982 (Exhibit 18) to the appellant admitting that the contract was to procure two new engines and the respondent No. 5 in association with the respondent No. 1 had imported the second-hand re-conditioned engines and that they shall remain responsible for any damage for unsatisfactory performance of the engines and make good the loss from their own resources and accordingly shall make repayment of BSRS loan strictly in accordance with repayment schedule and they shall be bound to compensate for the unsatisfactory performance of the reconditioned engines and shall indemnify the appellant for any loss, liability, harm or damage sustained or caused to the appellant on account of their non-fulfillment of the terms and conditions of the loan agreement or as may be imposed by the appellant at its absolute discretion. In this context it is pertinent to reproduce in verbatim for better appreciation the under-taking dated 14-12-1982 (Exhibit 18) which runs as follows:
"BANGLADESH SHILPA RIN SANGSTHA
(BSRS)
Agrani Bank Building
Motijheel C/A, Dhaka.
UNDERTAKING
Dear Sir, 
WHEREAS: 
i) You have granted to us She Shipping Lines Ltd a Company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913 and having our registered office at Previous 17, Siddeswari Lane, Presently: 1- F/3, Mirbagh, Nayatola, Moghbazar, Dhaka-17 a local currency loan of Taka 70,00,00 (Taka Seventy lakh) on terms and conditions contained in the Loan Agreement dated 6-6-1980 entered into between you and us and at our request placed work order to Rajdhani Ship Building & Engineering Works Ltd. Previously 5/1, Chittaranjan Avenue, Dhaka, Presently 23/1, East Rampura, Dhaka (hereinafter called the Dockyard) for construction of 2 Nos. Steel body self propelled cargo coaster(s)/Vessels of 600 DWT each on terms and conditions contained, in the Tripartite Contract No.  Nil dated 29-11-80 entered into among you, the said Dockyard and us (hereinafter called "Contract"). 
ii) In terms of para 7 of Annexure "A" to the said Contract it is required inter-alia, new engine (s) of reputable make in the said coaster(s) vessels are to be installed. 
iii) The Dockyard in association with us has imported the reconditioned engine(s) in place of brand new engine(s) stipulated in said contract. 
iv) For violation of the terms and conditions of the said Contract as aforesaid and as we are associated with the said violation you required from us an undertaking to the effect that we shall remain responsible for any damage/ unsatisfactory performance of the engiite(s) and make good the loss from our own resources and under no circumstance we shall disown BSRS loan liability and shall make repayment of BSRS loan strictly in accordance with the repayment schedule. 
12. Now, thereafter, we the said She Shipping Lines Ltd do in the premises agree, undertake and covenant as follows: 
1) That we shall remain responsible for any damage/unsatisfactory performance of the engine(s) installed in the Coaster(s)/Vessels built in the said Dockyard for us and make goodall the losses from our own resources and under no circumstance we will disown BSRS loan liability and shall make repayment of BSRS loan strictly in accordance with repayment schedule. 
2) That for any cause whatsoever the said engine (s) do not work satisfactorily we shall be completely liable for that and shall be bound to compensate for the said unsatisfactory performance. 
3) That in the event the engine(s) installed as aforesaid are absolutely damaged or absolutely incapable of giving satisfactory performance, on account of the same being Second-hand/recondition we shall be liable, on your demand, at your absolute discretion, to completely replace the said Second-hand/reconditioned engine(s) by brand new engine (s) immediately, 
4) That you shall at your discretion hold us responsible at any time for violation of the terms and conditions of the said Contract and/or the said Loan Agreement.
5) That this undertaking shall be without any prejudice to your rights and claims against us or as to your loans and we hereby confirm that we shall continue to repay your loans till liquidation thereof in terms of the Loan Agreement irrespective of any out come /result of such legal actions proceedings, 
6) This undertaking is additional and nothing /herein contained shall prejudice any of your rights or remedies in respect of any present or future security, obligation or decree for any of our indebtedness or liability. 
7) That we do hereby, further agree, undertake and covenant that we shall indemnify and keep you indemnified for any loss, liability harm or damage sustained, by or caused to you on account of our non fulfillment of the terms and conditions of the said con-tract and the Loan Agreement or as may be imposed by you at your absolute discretion. 
8) That we shall be absolutely abide by the aforementioned conditions. 
9) That this undertaking shall be binding on us and on our successors-in-interests, assigns, heirs, executors, administrators and legal representative. 
For and on behalf of
SHE SHIPPING LINES LIMITED.
1. Abdul Mabud Managing Director.
2. M Mokarram Hakim 
Director.
Dated, Dhaka 
the 14th December, 1982." 
13. The contents of this undertaking has been duly proved by the appellant and it acts as admission of the fact described therein by the respondent No.  1. section 58 of the Evidence Act, 1872 provides that facts admitted need not be proved. As per admission in the undertaking respondent No. 1 violated the terms and conditions of the tripartite contract entered into among the respondent Nos.1, 5 and the appellant. It also substantiates the claim of the appellant that the disbursement of the money of the 2nd installment was made with the full knowledge and under the instruction of the respondent No.  1 as opposed to the findings of both the trial Court as well as the High Court Division that respondent Nos.1 and 2 knew only of the disbursement of the first installment. It also appears that the High Court Division while holding that the second installment of the money was disbursed without the knowledge of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2, lost sight of the letter issued by the respondent No. 1 on 6-1-1981 (Exhibit 19) to the appellant requesting them to disburse the same to the respondent No. 5 the content of which has been duly proved by the appellant. 
14. We will now examine whether the respondent No. 1 is a loanee at law. What is loan or debt had been discussed by Lord Justice Lindley in the case Webb vs Stanton, (1883) 11 QBD 518 at page 527. He opined: 
      "I should say, apart from any authority, that a debt legal or equitable can be attached whether it be a debt owing or accruing; but it must be a debt, and a debt is a sum of money which is now        payable or will become payable in the future by reason of a present obligation debit in present solvendwn in future. An accruing debt, therefore, is a debt not yet actually payable, but a debt          which is represented by an existing obligation."
15. The Supreme Court of India in the case of National Royan Corporation Ltd vs Commissioner of Income Tax, AIR 1997 SC 3487 held as under: "The liability to repay arises the moment the money is borrowed. The amount borrowed may be repayable immediately or in future. The date of repayment of loan may be deferred by agreement but the obligation or the liability to repay will not cease on that account. The obligation is a present obligation; Debitum in Presenti, solvendum in futuro." 
16. It appears that to become a loanee or debtor a sum of money has to be borrowed or an obligation has to be accepted for which a sum of money is now payable or will become payable in future. In the instant case it is admitted that a loan agreement was executed between the appellant and the respondent No.  1. It is also not denied that the appellant made payment of Taka 28 lakh as second installment of the loan money to the account of respondent No. 5. It has been duly proved by the appellant that the money of second installment was advanced to the account of the respondent No. 5 at the request and with the full knowledge of the respondent No. 1. It is admitted fact that the first installment of money amounting to Taka 14 lakh was disbursed by the appellant for building the body of two vessels. After these two payments there is nothing left to make the respondent No. 1 borrower of the money.
17. In O'Driscoll vs Manchester Insurance Committee, (1915) 3 KB 499, the Court of Appeal held that where a panel doctor has done work under his agreement with the insurance committee, and the committee have received funds in respect of medical benefit from the National Insurance Commissioners, there is a debt owing or accruing from the insurance commit-tee to the panel doctor. Lord Justice Swinfen Eady observed at page 512 as under: 
"It is contended, however, that there cannot be a "debt" until the amount has been ascertained, and in support of this contention cases have been cited to us where it was attempted to attach unliqui dated damages. But in such cases there is no debt at all until the verdict of the jury is pronounced assessing the damages and judgment is given. Here is a debt, uncertain in amount, which will become certain when the accounts are finally dealt with by the Insurance Committee. Therefore there was a "debt" at the material date, though it was not presently payable and the amount was not ascertained. It is not like a case where there is a mere probability of a debt, as, for instance, where a person has to serve for a fixed period before being entitled to any salary, and he has served part of that period at the time the garnishee order Nisi is served. In such a case there is no "debt" until he has served the whole period." 
18. As observed in the preceding paragraph, this is also not a case where there exists a mere probability of a debt. In the instant case it is clearly a case of taking loan from the appellant and thereby incurring debt liability by the respondent No.  1 inasmuch as money was disbursed on request of the respondent No.  1 as per tripartite agreement to the respondent No. 5. Therefore, inevitably respondent No.  1 has become loanee at law. 
19. So, when money is disbursed on request of the respondent No. 1 as per tripartite con-tract to the respondent No.  5, inevitably respondent No. 1 becomes loanee at law and all con-sequential liabilities fall upon it. If that money is misappropriated by the respondent Nos. 5-7 that does not exempt respondent No. 1 from the loan liability. It is more so when seemingly fact of the misappropriation is known to the respondent No. 1 from the very beginning as evident from the undertaking given to the appellant by the respondent No.  1. 
20. Respondent No. 1 after giving under-taking to the effect that due to the violation of the contract by procuring two reconditioned engines instead of two new ones if any damage occurs they would make good the loss from their own resources, and accordingly make repayment of BSRS loan, they cannot be exempted from the responsibility as it appears that these two reconditioned engines have been lying in the godown of the Rupali Bank for clearance and the appellant has proved that 35% of construction of body of the vessels was completed by 14th March 1983 and thereafter there is no progress of the work though as per agreement the said vessels were required to be delivered within 31-10-1981. 
21. However, after the sanction of the loan there was a tripartite contract on 29-11-1980 between the BSRS-appellant and the respondent Nos.1 and 5. It has been stipulated in the contract that the installments were required to be paid to the respondent No. 5 builder in the dockyard and accordingly the appellant paid the said amount. But the mode of payment as stipulated in the tripartite contract was through letter of credit (LC). 
22. But it has to be noted that while disbursing the second installment amounting to Taka 28,000,00 (twenty eight lakh) the appellant advised for opening a letter of credit but the sponsor, respondent No. 1 did not pay heed to it. This advice was marked as Exhibit 15. The cheque was sent with the advice letter. From the conduct of the appellant it is evident that they did not violate the terms and conditions of the contract, rather non-cooperation of the respondent No. 1 resulted in the violation. So the liability does not fall upon the appellant. 
23. The appellant proved that the respondents are not at all interested to complete the project since the under-construction of the vessel had been left abandoned when the reconditioned engines were imported instead of new engines and thereby they violated the terms and conditions of the contract as well as the loan sanction letter. It has also been proved that the reconditioned engines were imported instead of new engines in the name of the respondent No. 5 not in the name of the appellant or the respondent No. 1 or the Project Company. By the conduct of the parties the appellant proved that the respondents failed to perform their part of the contract and make any payment of the outstanding loan and interest amounting to Taka 63,54,326.33 by 1-1-1984. 
24. As per Article 32 clause (b) of the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha Order, 1972 the violation of the terms and conditions of the loan agreement by the respondents has made the appellant entitled to have the repayment of the loan in full. Article 32 clause (b) of the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha Order, 1972 is reproduced below: 
"32. Notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, the Sangstha may, by notice, require any industrial concern to which it has granted any loan or any person who is liable for payment of such loan forthwith to repay the loan in full, if—
(a)   
(b) the industrial concern has failed to comply with the terms of any agreement with the Sangstha in the matter of the loan; or" 
25. From the aforesaid discussions and findings we are of the view that the appellant as petitioner in the miscellaneous case by adducing both oral and documentary evidence successfully proved their case for recovery of the present outstanding loan with interest of the respondents as on 1-1-1984 amounting to Taka 63,54,326.33. 
26. We also think it a proper case for awarding compensation for violation of contract by the respondents. In Sonali Bank vs M/s Karnaphuli Works Ltd, 2 BLT (AD) 78 = 46 DLR (AD) 55, this Division observed: 
"Section 34 of the CP Code provides that when the court passes a money decree, it may order interest to be paid on the principal sum adjudged from the date of the suit to the date of the decree, in addition to any interest adjudged on such principal sum for any period prior to the institution of the suit, with further interest on the aggregate sum so adjudged from the date of the decree to the date of payment. Purpose of this section has been expressed in a complex sentence, and if it is simplified, it will show that the court has got power to award interest for three distinct periods-(1) the period from the date a sum is payable to the date of institution of the suit, (2) the period during which the suit remains pending and (3) the period from the date of decree till payment of the decretal amount." 
27. In the aforesaid case his Lordship Justice Latifur Rahman, as he then was, further observed as under: "Section 73 of the Contract Act only speaks of compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of Contract. Thus, this section gives statutory recognition for compensation for any loss or damage Section 73 does not contemplate awarding of any interests by way of damage Strictly speaking under the law interest cannot be recovered as damages. Other than an agreement for the payment of interest at a fixed rate or it is payable by the usage of the trade having the force of law or under any substantive law." 
28. However, in Sonali Bank case (supra) trial court allowed an interest of Taka 33 lakh to the plaintiff for the period from the date the sum was payable to the date of institution of the suit, on the principal sum adjudged at a rate of 15% (the then bank interest rate) taking the ground that had the money due been kept in a bank as deposit, the plaintiff would have received interest to this extent and again allowed interest thereupon at a rate of 15% from the date of institution of the suit till realisation. The High Court Division concurred with the decision of the trial court excepting that the awarding of interest of Taka 33 lakh for the period prior to the institution of the suit was not interest, but compensation in the form of interest. This Division approved the decision holding that interest was not awarded by way of damages but the prevailing rate of bank interest was taken into consideration for measuring business loss and damages of the plaintiff and court is not prevented from adopting this method for determining the amount of compensation as per the existing bank rate. 
29. Article 33 clause (1)(d) of the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha Order, 1972 contemplates payment of "any other sum" relating to loan with the original loan money when the Sangstha becomes entitled to payment of any loan by reason of the breach of any condition of any agreement between the Sangstha and an industrial concern to which any loan has been granted. Article 33 clauses (1)(d) of the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha Order, 1972 is reproduced below: 
"33(1)—Where the Sangstha becomes entitled to require the immediate payment of any loan before the due date under Article 32 or by reason of the breach of any condition of any agreement between the Sangstha and an industrial concern to which any loan has been granted or any person liable for payment of that loan, or where an industrial concern to which any loan has been granted or any person liable for payment of that loan fails to repay the loan by the due date or in compliance with the notice under Article 32, an officer of the Sangstha generally or specially authorised by the Board in this behalf, may apply to the District Judge within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the industrial concern carries on the whole or a substantial part of its business, or the office or Branch of the Sangstha from which the loan was disbursed is situated, for one or more of the following reliefs, namely: 
(a) 
(b) 
(c)  
(d) an order for payment of the loan or any other sum relating thereto." 
30. Here the expression "any other sum" definitely connotes a sum adjudged as compensation for the breach of contract and to determine the extent of compensation existing bank rate of interest can be taken into consideration. 
Accordingly, the appeal is allowed with cost of Taka 20,000. The impugned judgment and order dated 4-6-2000 passed by the High Court Division in FMA No. 95 of 1990 is set-aside and the Miscellaneous Case No. 20 of 1986 is allowed. The respondents are directed to pay the aforesaid amount with a further compensation calculated at the rate of bank interest prevalent at the time of the institution of the suit. 
End.

full_judgment:
Md Ashfaqul Islam J : The Writ Petitioners 766 in numbers invoking this petition under Article 102 seek a direction upon the respondents to allow the benefits of two steps higher scale of pay with all arrears to them with effect from 1973 in the same manner as it has been done and created to the scale of clerks of Accounts department of the Bangladesh Railway since 1973. The Rule was issued in the following terms:

2. Let a Rule Nisi is issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why their inaction and failure to allow two steps higher scales to the petitioners since 1973 and the impugned Order dated 5-5-2009 as in (Annexure-G) shall not be declared to have been done without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and why a mandatory direction should not be issued upon them to allow two steps higher scales to the petitioners with effect from 1973, under the National Pay Scale of 1973 according to their entitlement on the basis of date of joining.

3. The background leading to the Rule, in short, is that the petitioners had joined in the services of Bangladesh Railway on different dates as Clerks ABC/Typist and subsequently promoted as Clerk Grade D and thereafter as Grade E and Grade-F respectively in the executive department. Some of them have already been promoted as Head Assistant, Welfare Inspector, Hours and Employment Regulation Inspectors from the post of Upper Division Assistant.

4. It has been stated that on the recommendations of the Martial Law Committee on Organizational set up of the Department/ Directorates/Sub-ordinate officers, popularity known as ENAM Committee the posts of the petitioners were renamed as Upper Division Assistant as a part of reorganization and restructuring of Bangladesh Railway and it was made the feeder post for the purpose of promotion in the post of Head Assistant, Welfare Inspector, Hours and Employment Regulation Inspectors. It is further stated that the post of Clerk Class-1 (CC-1), Clerk Class-II (CC-II) of the Accounts department were renamed and re-designated also as Upper Division Assistant and Lower Division Assistant respectively by the ENAM Committee.

5. In the Prescribed Pay Commission (PPC) 1949, the scale of the Clerk Grade-E was Taka 125-225 and Clerk Grade-F was in the scale of Taka 160-250. Under the Revised Pay Scale- 1963 the scale of the Clerk Grade-E was Taka 185-315 and Clerk Grade-F was in the scale of Taka 235-340. Under the National Pay Scale- 1973 the scale of the Clerk Grade-E was Taka 310-670 and Clerk Grade-F was also in the scale of Taka 310-670. Under the New National Pay Scale-1977 both of them were allowed the same scale of Taka 400-825 and under the National Pay Scale- 2005 they were allowed the corresponding scale of Taka 3,500-7,500.

6. On the other hand, the Clerk Class-1 of the Accounts department of the Bangladesh Railway was in the scale of Taka 75-150 under the PPC- 1949, Taka 135-315 under the Revised Pay Scale- 1963. Though their status was at the two stage lower level and getting lower scales under the previous two pay scales than the petitioners but suddenly in 1973 they were upgraded at the two stage higher level and was given the same scale as was allowed to the petitioners i.e. the scale of Taka 310-670 in the then Grade- VII. The said decision was ex-facie illegal and without lawful authority. The railway was under legal obligation to upgrade the scales of the petitioners in the same manner at the two stage higher level as had been done in the cases of Clerk Class-I of the Accounts department. The scales of the petitioners were not upgraded without any rhyme or reason.

7. In this way in 1973 by upgrading the scale of the Clerk Class-I of the Accounts department the Government had treated unequals equally and it was done to allow a benefit to a group of people. Placing the Clerk Class-I of the Accounts department with the petitioners who had although been the lower scale and status then the Clerk Class-I of the Executive department was discriminatory, arbitrary by which the present petitioners had been adversely affected and prejudiced. The Clerk Class-I of the Accounts department were not doing similar and identical jobs to the petitioners rather they were doing less laborious and important works in the Accounts department. In 1973 the Government had committed a serious illegality by treating dissimilarly people similarly in violation of the provisions of the Constitution and the services (Re-organization & Conditions) Act, 1975 [Act No. XXXII of 1975]. It is further stated that denial of the benefit of upgradation of scales of the petitioners was illegal, mala fide, unwarranted, and without any lawful authority.

8. It has been further stated that the long standing issue of disparity of pay of the petitioners had been repeatedly brought to the notice of the authority of the Government by the petitioners themselves and the different organizations of the employees of Bangladesh Railway. But no action was taken. It is further stated that instead of removing disparity and discrimination of pay of the petitioners with the others similarly situated employees, the respondents vide an Order dated 17-1-1985 under Office Order No. R/Esttb.-8/84-12 issued by the Director/Deputy Secretary (Finance), Railway Division, Ministry of Communication, the post of Upper Division Assistant of the Accounts department of the Bangladesh Railway was re-designated as Auditor but no step for re-designation of the Upper Division Assistants of the Executive department i.e. the petitioners was taken. It is the second time the petitioners had been the victim of serious injustice and discrimination. The persons who were junior to them and also getting lower scale under Prescribed Pay Commission- 1949 and Revised Pay Scale- 1963 were given a benefit of upgradation of scale at the two Stage higher level in 1973 first and in 1985 for the second time those persons were illegally again granted higher status. The acts of the respondents were worst form of favouritism in favour of one group and discrimination against the other group who although had been holding higher pay, rank and status than the CC-I of the Accounts Department.

9. It has been further brought to our notice that the Government had promulgated জেলা ও উপজেলা অফিসের কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারীদের নিয়োগ বিধি ১৯৮৬ vide SRO No. 133-L/86 which was notified in the official Gazette on 28-4-1986 (Annexure-B). In the said SRO the upper Division Assistants of the District and Upazilla offices who were getting the scale of Taka 325-610 in Grade-XVI of the New National Pay Scale-1977 were allowed the corresponding scale of Taka 750-155 under the amended National Pay Scale 1985 in Grade-XVI. Similarly the Head Assistants of the District and Upazilla Offices who were getting the scale of Taka 370-745 in Grade-XV of New National Pay Scale- 1977 were allowed the scale of Taka 800-1,630 in Grade-XIV under the amended National Pay Scale 1985. It is manifestly clear that the Upper Division Assistants and Head Assistants working in the District and Upazilla level were granted the scales in Grade-XV and XIV respectively under the amended National Pay Scale-1985, but on the other hand, the petitioners who are the Upper Division Assistants, Head Assistants of the Railway and UDAs were already in the scale of Grade-XII Taka 850-1700 and the Head Assistants were in the scale of Taka 900-2075 under amended National Pay Scale-1985 were kept in the same scale in clear violation of their legal rights.

10. It is also stated that in the above circumstances the petitioners filed an application to the respondent No. 3 on 9-1-2007 for upgradation of the Pay Scales of the Upper Division Assistants from Grade- XIII to Grade-XI i.e. from Taka 3,500-7,500 to Taka 4,100-8,820 and Pay Scale of the Head Assistants from Grade-XI to Grade-X i.e. Taka 5,100-10,360 under the National Pay Scale-2005.

11. Then again on 17-1-2007 vide letter No. E-3/Pay-1/2007-13 the office of the respondent No. 3 had asked the General Managers (East and West) of the Bangladesh Railway to send detailed information in a prescribed table to remove the disparity of pay of the petitioners and by letter dated 6-3-2007 the General Manager (West) of the Bangladesh Railway had asked the all concerned departments to send those detailed information to him and accordingly on receipt of those information from the concerned offices of the Railway and the General Managers, the respondent No. 3 vide letter No. E-3 /Pay-1 /2007-699 dated 15-8-2007 had sent those information and requested the respondent No. 1 to obtain sanction from the Ministry of Finance to remove the disparity of the pay of the petitioners and other Head Assistants, Upper Division Assistants and Lower Division Assistants. In his letter he had categorically stated the matters of serious injustice done to the petitioners without any reason (Annexure-D series).

12. In reply to the letter dated 17-4-2008 issued by the respondent No. 1, the respondent No. 3 again had sent a comparative statement of discrimination and disparity of pay of the petitioners with the Auditors on 29-4-2008 vide letter No. E-3 /pay-1/2007-154. The Secretary, Ministry of Communication on 15-5-2008 had sent a summary to the Secretary, Ministry of Finance seeking his approval for removing disparity and discrimination of pay of the petitioners which was forwarded by his office on 22-5-2008 (Annexure-E & E-1).

13. Persuasion went on. On 26-10-2008 the secretary of Finance had requested the respondent No. 1 to send some additional information including recruitment Rules of the Auditors of the Accounts department of Bangladesh Railway for taking necessary steps for upgradation of the pay scales of the petitioners. In reply to the said letter the office of the General Manager (East) on 8-2-200 vide letter No. 80-E/211/Pay-Anomaly (loose-1) (CP) had sent the detailed and comparative statement again as per requirement of the Ministry of Finance which was subsequently forwarded to the Ministry of Finance for necessary action by the respondent No. 1 (Annexure-F & F-1).

14. In fine, as it has been stated in the petition that after long deliberation when the petitioners were expecting to get their entitled upgraded scale suddenly like a bolt from the blue the Ministry of Finance vide a letter dated 5-5-2009 under Memo No. (যোগাযোগ ৪/২০০৮/৮১) passed the impugned Order (Annexure-G) which is as follows:—

“নির্বাহী বিভাগের বর্তমান উচ্চমান সহকারী ও প্রধান সহকারী দুটি পদই কমন ক্যাটাগরীর পদ এবং সরকারের সকল অফিসে এ সকল পদে একই বেতনস্কেল নির্ধারিত রয়েছে। এক্ষুনে শুধুমাত্র রেলওয়ের ক্ষেত্রে প্রস্তাবিত বেতনস্কেল উন্নীত করা হলে সরকারের অন্যান্য সকল অফিসে বিদ্যমান একইরুপ পদ হতে বেতনস্কেল উন্নীতকরনের প্রস্তাব আসবে। যাতে সরকারের বেতন কাঠামোতে অসামঞ্জস্যতা দেখা দিবে। তবে পদ সৃষ্টির কাল থেকে যেহেতু নির্বাহী বিভাগের বিবেচ্য পদসমূহ ভিন্ন পদ নামে তুলনীয় হিসাব বিভাগ হতে উচ্চতর পদ ও বেতনস্কেলে বিদ্যমান ছিল সেহেতু প্রশাসনিক মন্ত্রনালয় কর্তৃক প্রয়োজন মনে করলে হিসাব বিভাগের ন্যায় নির্বাহী বিভাগের বিবেচ্য পদও সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রনালয় ও অর্থ বিভাগের মনিটরিং সেল এর সম্মতিক্রমে পদ বিন্যাস অনুযায়ী উন্নীত যোগ্যতা/অভিজ্ঞতায় পদনাম পরিবর্তনের বিষয়ে প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করতে পারেন। নির্বাহী বিভাগের বর্তমান পদনামে প্রস্তাব অনুযায়ী বেতনস্কেল উন্নীতকরনের কোন সুযোগ নাই।

15. The respondents had refused to upgrade the scales of the petitioners on the ground that it would create further anomaly in the pay structure of the Government and had advised to the effect that the name of the posts of the petitioners might be upgraded or renamed. The Order was ex-facie illegal and without lawful authority and violative of the provisions of the Services (Re-organization & Conditions) Act, 1975 [Act No. XXXII of 1975]. The said Order is also ultra vires to the provisions of the said Act (Annexure-G). It is at this stage the petitioners moved this Division under Article 102 the Constitution and obtained the present Rule. On the doctrine of equality and equal protection of Law this petition has been preferred by the Officers and Employees who were discriminated in fixation of their pay scale.

16. Mr Md Salahuddin (Dolon) appearing with Mr Omar Farooq, the learned Counsel for the petitioners after placing the petition, impugned Order and the relevant Annexures with the petition has made an exhaustive and elaborate argument touching upon the points and merits of the case by contending the salient feature of the Constitution safe guarding the equality principle as enshrined in the Constitution. Mr Dolon pays particular emphasize by drawing our notice to the impugned Order (Annexure-G) wherein it has been admitted by the Ministry of Finance in the following manner:

“(ক) প্রথমতঃ এনাম কমিটি কর্তৃক নির্বাহী বিভাগের উচ্চতর স্কেল ও পদবিশিষ্ট উভয়কে একই পদনামে ও বেতন স্কেলে নামকরণ এবং

(খ) দ্বিতীয়ঃ শুধুমাত্র হিসাব বিভাগের উক্ত উচ্চমান সহকারী পদকে আবার অডিটর পদনামে পরিবর্তন করে উন্নীত বেতনস্কেল প্রদান করার কারনে এবং নির্বাহী বিভাগের বিবেচ্য পদের বেতনস্কেল উন্নীত না করার কারনে তুলনীয় হিসাব বিভাগের সাথে নির্বাহী বিভাগের বিবেচ্য পদসমূহের বেতনস্কেলে বৈষম্যর সৃষ্টি হয়েছে মর্মে দেখা যায়।”

17. The learned Counsel further submits that through this is a positive observation on the part of the Ministry of Finance but unfortunately, the Ministry denied upgrading the pay scale of the petitioners without any valid and cogent reason. After the admission of the Ministry of Finance, as he submits there is no legal bar to upgrade the pay scale of the petitioners according to their entitlement. Therefore, the learned Counsel most humbly submits that this a very modest, reasonable and innocuous prayer on the part of the employees those who have been deprived from entitlement of the proper pay scale in the manner as it has been already stated.

18. Mr Dolon cited several decisions on the development of the service laws. propounded by the Appellate Division and this Division. He also cited the decision of the Indian Supreme Court on the point. Pith and substance of these decisions is mainly on the point of maintainability of the Writ Petition in the present form. The decisions are: Dr Nurul Islam vs Secretary, Ministry of Health and Population Control, 33 DLR (AD) 201, Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh 44 DLR (AD) 111, Secretary, Ministry of Establishment vs Shafiuddin Ahmed, 50 DLR (AD) 27, Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretanj, Ministry of Finance vs Md Abdur Rashid, 12 BLC (AD) 142, Delwar Hossain Mia vs Bangladesh, 52 DLR (AD) 120, Government of Bangladesh vs Md Shamsul Huq 59 DLR (AD) 54 and Mahbubul Alam vs Bangladesh, 61 DLR 728, as well as five unreported decisions.

19. In an unreported decision of Station Master and Karmachari Union represented by its President Bangladesh Railway, Kamalapur, Dhaka vs Bangladesh in Writ Petition No. 7332 of 2005 this Division considering the disparity of pay scale entertained the Writ Petition holding the same to be maintainable and made the rule absolute directing the respondent to allow the employees of Bangladesh Railway who are the member of Union (the petitioners in that case), a higher scale with all arrear, pay and other benefits due from 1977, Mr Dolon submits that the petitioners in the present case standing on the same footing also making a claim in the same manner on the plea of disparity of pay scale on the ground of violation of equality principle of the Constitution.

20. On the other hand, Mr Shaheed Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 3 Director General, Bangladesh Railway by filing affidavit-in-opposition vehemently opposes the Rule on several grounds. Firstly, he argued that this Writ Petition is not maintainable since all the petitioners are in Government service and their pay scale have been included under the terms and condition of their service which comes under the purview of Article 117 of the Constitution. Their forum is Administrative Tribunal. On this point he mainly placed reliance in the decision of Mujibur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh 44 DLR (AD) 111.

21. Next he submits that long delay in filing the Writ Petition has vitiated the claim of the petitioners. He relied on 52 DLR (AD) 112 on the point. Next he submits relying on the decision of Union of India vs Pradip Kumar Dey 8 SCC (2000) 580 that mere recommendation by Directorate of CRPF to the pay commission did not entitled any member of CRPF to a  mandamus to enforce such recommendation. In that case it was held that mere recommendation did not confer any right on the respondent to make such a claim in writ of mandamus. Thus he submits that the foundation of argument of the learned Counsel for the petitioner on that score does not merit any substance. He also submits that it would be difficult to ascertain the individual entitlement of the petitioners and to decide what would be their pay scale in furtherance of their respective claim. Basing on these grounds the learned Counsel finally concludes that this rule is devoid of any substance, which should be discharged outright.

22. Heard the learned Advocate for both sides at length and considered their submissions. In our anxiety, we have meticulously gone through the petition, all the Annexures with it, affidavit-in-opposition and other materials on record.

23. The moot question that faces this Division in this Writ Petition is whether under the facts and circumstances of the present case, the petitioners are entitled to have higher scale with effect from 1973 under the National Pay Scale of 1973 according to their entitlement on the basis of date of joining (this is the core issue to be addressed in this Writ Petition).

<u>24. Article 117(3) of the Constitution provides hat no Court shall entertain any proceeding or make any Order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of an Administrative Tribunal. 'Court' has been defined in Article 152 of the Constitution that includes the Supreme Court and hence I normally the High Court Division should not entertain any Writ Petition in respect of any matter falling within jurisdiction of any Administrative Tribunal. But there is an exception where the High Court Division can also entertain Writ Petition of a kind upon a view that the remedy before the Administrative Tribunal is not efficacious or that under the particular facts and circumstances of the cases the Writ Petition can be entertained, notwithstanding availability of alternative remedy before the Tribunal. In this context we would like to discuss a decision cited by Mr Dolon which is the case of Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Finance vs Md Abdur Rashid, 12 BLC (AD) 142. In that decision the Appellate Division upheld the decision of the High Court Division. High Court Division made the Rule absolute declaring the petitioners of that case, who were serving as employees in the different categories in the Appellate Division and the High Court Division of Supreme Court of Bangladesh to be treated at par with the accountants serving in different Ministries of the Government in respect of scale of pay and granting selection grade. The Appellate Division while upholding the decision of the High Court Division came down heavily on the issue and observed. "Be that as it may, the main contention raised on their behalf is that the respondents being Government servants the writ petition is not maintainable there being other remedy available to them before the Administrative Tribunal. It appears that the persistent case advanced on behalf of the respondents is that they have been discriminated in the matter of fixation of pay scale and granting of selection grade and their fundamental right of equal treatment as enshrined in the Constitution being violated they had no other  alternative but to move the High Court Division its writ jurisdiction as they could, not ventilate the grievance of violation of their fundamental rights before the  Administrative Tribunal. The wrong complained of being inextricably mixed up, in our opinion, the High Court Division was justified to lay its hand in writ jurisdiction for prevention of injury and vindication of justice and to protect fundamental rights of enjoying equal protection of law and equal opportunity of the writ petitioners in their employment there being flagrant violation of the rights."</u>

25. Appellate Division further observed:—

"With the aforesaid observation the High Court Division came to a clear finding that the writ petitioners have been discriminated against being deprived of equal opportunity in their employment and also their fundamental rights of having equality before law and equal protection of law has been violated and, as such, made the Rule absolute."

26. Another employee if the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, Md Shamsul Huq got remedy in the High Court Division and he Rule was made absolute on the ground of Shamsul Huq being discriminated from the personal officers of the Secretariat. By granting leave against the said decision at the instance of the Government of Bangladesh, the Appellate Division dismissed the Appeal in Bangladesh vs Md Shamsul Huq. The Appellate Division held:—

"we are of the view that the respondent and Personal Officers of the Secretariat having been similarly situated have been discriminated and cannot be treated differently and is repugnant to the equality doctrine and, under like circumstances and conditions, should be treated alike both in their rights and privilege."

27. Further Justice Tafazzul Islam in that decision observed:— "Since the writ petitioner' relief could not have been obtained by a supplemental role performed by the Tribunals the writ petitions have rightly invoked the jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102(1) of the Constitution and so the Writ Petitions were fully maintainable. As it appears, the principle as laid down in 50 DLR (AD) 27, in the facts and circumstances, are applicable in the present Appeal as the writ petitioners challenged the Orders as contained in Annexures D (1) and D (2), which were issued under section 5 of the Services (Re-organisation and Conditions) Act 1975 and have the effect of law. Accordingly, the writ petition is maintainable."

28. So, it appears that in a fit case where absolute question of infringement of any violation of Constitutional provision specially when the violation is of such kind that it has directly infringed the right of a citizen that has been protected expressly by the Constitution, in such a case there should not be any hindrance or obstacle of alternative remedy and certainly Writ is maintainable.

29. Mr Shaheed Alam brought to our notice the decision reported in 85 SCC as referred to above and made his submissions. Our view is that the submissions do not hold good in the context of our Constitution. The Indian context is different. In Mujibur Rahnum's Case as referred to above (44 DLR) it has been observed:

"Within its jurisdiction the Tribunal can strike down an Order for violation of principles of natural justice as well as for infringement of fundamental rights, guaranteed by the Constitution, or any other law, in respect of matters relating to or arising of sub-clause (a), but such tribunals cannot, like the Indian Administrative Tribunals in exercise of a more comprehensive jurisdiction under Article 323A (see SP Sampath Kumar vs Union of India, AIR 1937 SC 386 (Para 16) and JB Chopra vs Union of India AIR 1987 SC 357 (Para 2), strike down any law or Rule on the ground of its constitutionality. A person in the service of the Republic who intends to invoke fundamental right for challenging the vires of a law will seek his remedy under Article 102(1), but in all other cases be will he required to seek remedy under Article 117 (2)"

30. From the above citation, we could find that the Indian Administrative Tribunal exercises more comprehensive jurisdiction under Article 323 A of their Constitution. Indian Constitution under Article 323A gives following jurisdiction:

"Administrative Tribunal—(1) Parliament may, by law, provide for the adjudication or trial by administrative tribunals of disputes and complaints with respect to recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of any State or of any local or other authority within the territory of India or under the control of the government of Indian or of any corporation owned or controlled by the Government.

(2) A law made under clause (1) may—

(a) Provide for the establishment of an administrative tribunal for the Union and a separate administrative tribunal for each State or for two or more States;

(b) Specify the Jurisdiction, powers (including the power to punish for contempt) and authority which may be exercised by each of the said tribunals;

(c) Provide for the procedure (including provisions as to limitation and rules of evidence) to be followed by the said tribunals;

(d) Exclude the jurisdiction of all Courts, except the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under article 136, with respect to the disputes or complaints referred to in clause (1);

(e) Provide for the transfer to each such administrative tribunal of any cases pending before any Court or other authority immediately before the establishment of such tribunal as would have been within the jurisdiction of such tribunal if the causes of action on which such suits or proceedings are based had arisen after such establishment; (f) repeal or amend any Order made by the President under clause (3) of Article 371D;

(g) contain such supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions (including provisions as to fees) as Parliament may deem necessary for the effective functioning of, and for the speedy disposal of cases by, and the enforcement of the Orders of, such tribunals."

31. Further sub-section (3) states:—

"(3) The provisions of this article shall have effect notwithstanding anything in any other provision of this Constitution or in any other law for the time being in force."

32. Our administrative tribunal does not have such an wider jurisdiction like that of India. It does not even have jurisdiction to pass any ad-interim Order. Jurisprudence is developing and changing rapidly to meet the present day situation. In that perspective the decision in 12 BLC (AD) and 59 DLR (AD) referred to above is absolutely correct and we are in respectful agreement with the same. Therefore, by inducting the principle enunciated in the case reported by the learned counsel for the respondent 8SCC we cannot debar the petitioners holding considering facts and circumstances of the present case a mandamus cannot be resorted to simply saying that the basis of the claim of the petitioners are on the basis of the recommendations made by different ministries only. The Bangladesh Railway now has its own Ministry and having a ministry of their own certainly it can take an independent decision. Things would now become much easier to resolve the question that faces this Division on the basis of the claim of the petitioners.

33. As we have mentioned at the outset that already this Division in the unreported decision, i.e. Writ Petition No. 7332 of 2005, considering the claim of the petitioners of the case who stand on the same footing like that of the petitioners in the case in hand, (the petitioners were the employees of the Railway) allowed the Higher scale and arrear pay and other benefits. We cannot discriminate the petitioners before us standing on the same footing, claiming the same right which has been declared in favour of the petitioner in the said Writ Petition.

34. Every citizen should be treated in accordance with law and only in accordance with the Law, is the saying of the Constitution and in many a decision this Constitutional saying has been reflected time and again to combat a situation where owing to discrimination or disparity a right of a citizen has been disregarded. Fortified with all the decision, the submissions we are of the view that this Rule should succeed.

35. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without cost. The respondents are hereby directed to consider the petitioners claims and allow them to have higher scale since 1973 under the national Pay Scale 1973 according to their entitlement on the basis of date of joining with immediate effect, however, among the petitioners who would not be entitled or qualify otherwise to have the same higher scale as claimed should also be considered by the respondents at the same time. This Order should be implemented as expeditiously as possible.

Communicate at once.

End.

parties:
Ibrahim (Md) and ors ------ Petitioners
Vs
Ratan Chandra Nath & anr ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule calls in question the legality and propriety of the judgment and order dated 1-4-2001 passed by the learned Additional Divisional Commissioner, Chittagong, in Civil Appeal (Rangamati) No. 6 of 1997, allowing the appeal by reversing the judgment and order dated 25-11-1996 passed by the learned Deputy Commissioner, Rangamati in Civil Suit No. 5 of 1994, dismissing the suit.

2. Short facts leading to this Rule, are that on 19-4-1994, the opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Civil Suit No. 5 of 1994 in the Court of Deputy Commissioner, Rangamati, impleading the petitioners and opposite party No. 2 as defendants for ejectment of the defendants from the suit premises described in the schedule of the plaint.

3. The plaintiff's case put in a nutshell is that he is the sole owner of the property described in the schedule of the plaint as District Rangamati, Police Station Kawkhali of 98 Kachukhali Mouja, Khatian Nos. 358 plot No. 2522. The nature of the suit premises is the bamboo made shop. He permitted the defendants to take shelter in the said premises for a temporary period. Taking such advantage the defendants are staying in the said premises. On repeated requests the defendants failed to deliver the vacant possession of the same to him, rather on 12-2-1994 the defendants made extension around the premises without his prior permission. On 28-1-1994, the defendants lastly refused to deliver the possession to him. Hence, the suit.

4. The defendants appeared in the suit and repeatedly took adjournment to file the written statement but subsequently, the defendants did not file the written statement.

5. Eventually, the suit came up for hearing before the learned Deputy Commissioner, Rangamati who by the judgment and order dated 25-11-1996 dismissed the suit. On appeal the learned Additional Divisional Commissioner, by the judgment and order dated 1-4-2001 passed in Civil Appeal (Rangamati) No. 6 of 1997 allowed the appeal and reversed the judgment of the trial Court.

6. Feeling aggrieved the defendants as petitioners preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr Md Bashiruddin Zindigir, the learned Advocate appearing with Md Salahuddin, Advocate, seeks to impeach the impugned judgment and order on the two-fold arguments. Firstly, the suit is not maintainable in its present form, inasmuch as the plaintiff without seeking any relief for declaration of title filed the instant suit. Secondly, earlier the predecessor of the plaintiff filed Civil Suit No. 21 of 1990 over the self-same land which was subsequently dismissed but the Court of appeal below did not at all consider the consequence of the same. He adds that without taking evidence and without reversing the finding of facts arrived at by the trial Court the Court of appeal below passed the impugned judgment which caused serious miscarriage of justice. In support of his contention the learned Counsel refers the case of Johara Khatun and others vs Md Habib Khan and another reported in 1995 BLD (AD) 120 wherein it is held that:

"While exercising revisional power under section 115, CPC the High Court Division usually does not go into questions of fact. But when the appellate Court reverses the judgment of the trial Court on non-consideration of the material evidence on record and without adverting to the reasons on which the trial Court based its judgment, the High Court Division may be justified in interfering with the finding of facts arrived at by the appellate Court when it finds that non-consideration of such evidence has materially affected the decision of the appellate Court occasioning failure of justice."

8. The learned Counsel further refers the case of Babru Mia vs Md Abul Kashem being dead his heirs: Mrs Nurjahan Begum and others reported in 4 BLT (AD) 223 wherein it is held:

"We have gone through the judgments of both the trial Court and the High Court Division. The High Court Division has rightly taken the view that the title of the plaintiff to the suit property is itself clouded and the registered lease deed Exhibit 1 was not acted upon, inasmuch as admittedly, there was no payment of rent in terms as the said lease deed. The suit therefore involved a serious question of title and in the absence of a proper suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession a simple SCC suit under the circumstances does not lie."

9. The learned Counsel further refers the provisions of Order VII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and submits that this Rule provides that where the subject-matter of the suit is immovable property, the plaint shall contain a description of the property sufficient to identify it, and, in case such property can be identified by boundaries or numbers in a record of settlement of survey, the plaint shall specify such boundaries or numbers. The learned Counsel lastly submits that the Court of appeal below failed to weigh and sift the materials on record as required by law and evidently fell in an error in coming to his ultimate decision occasioning failure of justice.

10. Mr Parimal Chandra Guha, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Samiran Mallik, Advocate for the opposite party No. 1, opposes the Rule and submits that the learned Judge of the trial Court did not consider the materials on record, thereby came to an erroneous decision which caused serious miscarriage of justice. He adds that the suit property belongs to the plaintiff and the defendants did not challenge the title of the plaintiff, so the suit for ejectment without seeking declaration is maintainable. The learned Counsel further submits that the Court of appeal below considered the provisions of law laid down in Order XLI, rule 31 of the CPC and by reversing the finding of facts arrived at by the trial Court rightly passed the impugned judgment. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel refers the case of Haidernessa and another vs Monowara Begum and others reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 280 wherein it is held:

"The High Court Division found that the lower appellate Court fully considered the oral and documentary evidence of the parties, believed the plaintiffs case and came to a finding that the defendants illegally dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit lands on 29-1-1970 and, as such, the suit was filed within time. The difference between the judgments of the trial Court and the lower appellate Court being one of appreciation of evidence, the High Court Division had little scope to interfere with the findings of the final Court of facts based on evidence."

11. The learned Counsel further refers the case of Hazari Bala Sana and another vs Niron alias Niranjan Mandal and others reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 294 wherein it is held:

"It is a settled principle that the findings of fact, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court, which is the final Court of fact, is binding on the High Court Division, as a revisional Court except in certain well defined exceptional circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence affecting the merit of the case.

In the instant case, from the judgment of the appellate Court, it is found that in arriving at its findings the said Court carefully considered all the material facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, inclusive of the registered Kabuliyats, RS and SA Khatians, registered sale deeds and rent receipts and consequently, these findings of facts are immune from attack in revision."

12. The learned Counsel lastly submits that upon considering the materials on record, the Court of appeal below rightly reversed the judgment of the trial Court which calls for no interference by this Court.

13. In order to appreciate the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels, I have gone through the revisional application, along with other materials on record and given my anxious consideration to their submissions.

14. Now, the question that calls for consideration is, whether the Court of appeal below committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment and order dated 1-4-2001 passed by the Court of appeal below.

<u>15. At the very outset, it will be pertinent to mention that the Regulation No. 4(2) of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulation, 1900 (Regulation No. 1 of 1900) provides that.</u>

<u>No other enactment, heretofore or hereafter, passed shall be deemed to apply in the Chittagong Hill Tracts:</u>

<u>Provided that the Government may, by notification in the (Official Gazette)—</u>

<u>(a) declare that any other enactment shall apply in the said tracts, either wholly or to the extent or with the modification which may be set forth in the notification, or</u>

<u>(b) declare that any enactment which is specified in the schedule, or which has been declared to apply by a notification under clause(a) of this sub-section, shall cease to apply in the said tracts.</u>

16. In view of the aforesaid Provisions, the Code of Civil Procedure is not applicable in the Chittagong Hill Tracts i.e. Rangamati and other two hill districts. Therefore, the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the petitioners in respect of applicability of the Code of Civil Procedure is repelled.

17. Ongoing through the materials on record, it appears that the Court of appeal below considered the khatian No. 358 and the rent receipts furnished by the plaintiff which show that the right, title and possession belongs to the plaintiff. Moreover, the defendants did not challenge the title of the plaintiff by filing any written statement. So, it is admitted that the defendants were in permissive possession in the suit premises. Therefore, in my view, the title of the plaintiff has not been clouded. It further appears to me that the Court of appeal below reversed the finding of facts arrived at by the trial Court to the effect that the Title Suit No. 21 of 1990 was a suit for permanent injunction filed by the plaintiff and the same was dismissed for default. So, the same does not lead to any inference that the plaintiff has no title in the suit premises. It further appears to me that the findings arrived at by the Court of appeal below having been rested upon consideration and discussion of legal evidence and materials on record and also on a correct and proper analysis of the legal aspects involved in the case and the findings being a finding of facts are not liable to be disturbed by the High Court Division in exercise of the power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this regard, reliance is being placed in the cases reported in 43 DLR (AD) 82, 51 DLR (AD) 57, 1999 BLD (AD) 156 and 38 DLR (AD) 201.

18. Having regard to the facts, I find that all the matters in dispute in the case have rightly been considered and decided by the Court of appeal below with reference to the materials on record. Moreover, I do not find any misreading or non-consideration of the materials on record. The impugned judgment and order passed by the Court of appeal below are well reasoned backed by sufficient materials on record which cannot be interfered. Therefore, I failed to discover any merit in the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the petitioners. I have gone through the decisions as referred by the learned Counsel for the petitioners, I am in respectful agreement with the principles enunciated therein but the facts leading to those cases are quite distinguishable with that of the instant case. So, his submissions are repelled as being devoid of any substance. On the contrary, the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the opposite party No. 1 prevails and appears to have a good deal of force.

<u>19. In view of the aforesaid observations, I hold that the people of the Hill Districts of Chittagong are the citizens of this Republic and all laws which are now in force in Bangladesh should be equally applicable to the Hill Districts of Chittagong and in order to give benefit of those laws to the inhabitants of those areas, it is high time for the Executive Organ of the State to take necessary steps for setting up of Civil and Criminal Courts as per provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 forthwith and apply all other laws of the country to that area without any let or hindrance.</u>

20. In view of the discussion made above and the preponderant judicial views emerging out of the authorities referred to above I am of the view that the impugned judgment and order suffer from no illegality or impropriety which calls for no interference by this Court. Thus, the Rule having no merit fails.

21. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

Send down the records of this case at once with a copy of the judgment.

End.
