full_judgment:
Md. Ashfaqul Islam J : At the instance of the petitioner Redwan Ahmed, this Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the proceeding of Metro Bishesh Case No.133 of 2007 arising out of Ramna Police Station Case No. 40 dated 15-2-2007 filed under section 409 of the Penal Code 1860, in respect of an offence allegedly committed on 11-6-2002 read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, now on transfer, pending before the learned Special Judge Court No.2, Dhaka, should not he declared to be without lawful authority, in as much as the transfer, as made, is in violation of Rule-18ka of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, and since hits the provisions of Article 35 of the Constitution read with Article 26 of the Constitution.

2. Back ground leading to the issuance of the Rule, in short, is that one Md. Nurul Islam Babu of village-Mopdhya Pashchim Kamargaon, Police Station Srinagar, District Munshiganj, lodged a First Information Report with the Officer-in-Charge of Ramna Police Station, Dhaka Metropolitan Police, Dhaka on 15-2-2007 against the petitioner and two others showing the date of occurrence on 19-6-2002 alleging inter alia that the 4% of the amount received against lease money of hat-bazer of the country under the Ministry of Local Government was deposited with the Muktijoddah Sangsad account to be spent for the welfare of distressed and unemployed freedom fighters through the Bangladesh Muktijoddah Sangsad Central Command Council, Dhaka (hereinafter referred to as "the Muktijoddha Council); the amount thus collected stood at approximately TK.5,00, 00,000 (five core) and it was deposited with a Bank account opened with the Sonali Bank, Moghbazar Branch, Dhaka by the Muktijoddha Council.

3. In the year 2002 while the then Chairman, Mr Redwan Ahmed and the then Finance Secretary (at present Secretary General) Shah Alam Chowdhury of Muktijoddha Council were the custodian of the Muktijoddha Council, at he instance of the then Vice-Chairman (at present Chairman) Md Kabir Ahmed, without any organization's approval by abuse of their powers withdrew Taka 50,00,000 (Taka fifty lakh) from the said Bank account vide Cheque No.1474231 dated 11-6-2002 for an amount of Taka 20,00,000; cheque No.1474214 dated -11-6-2002 for an amount of Taka 20,00,000 and cheque No.1474215 dated 11-6-2002 for an amount of Taka 10,00,000 and misappropriated the same without spending for the interest of Muktijoddha.

4. It was also stated in the alleged FIR that prior to resignation from the post of Chairman, Redwan Ahmed paid Taka 20,00,000 to Kabir Ahmed and Shah Alam in presence of present Vice Chairman Shafiqul Islam Robi and member Sattar Shaheb of the Muktijoddha Council in presence of the informant but Kabir Ahmed and Shah Alam distributed the total amount of Taka 50 lakh including the said Taka 20 lakh amongst them never returned or deposited the said amount of Taka 50 lakh to the Council. The audit authority recommended for taking appropriate action against the accused persons but no action was taken by the Council Authority to cover up their own illegal act. Upon above allegations Ramna Police Station Case No. 40 dated 15-2-2007 under section 409 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947 was started against the petitioner and others.

5. The FIR has been lodged under section 409 of the Penal Code and the same being a scheduled offence of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2004 was investigated into by the Anti-Corruption Commission (herein after referred to as ACC). The ACC investigated into the case and during investigation recorded the statement of the witnesses, collected the material on record, and after investigation submitted the Memo of evidence before the ACC. After obtaining sanction under section 32 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2004 the investigation officer submitted charge sheet before the Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka being charge sheet No.526 dated 8-10-2007 under section 409 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947. The case record was then transmitted to the Court of Mahanagar Senior Special Judge, Dhaka and the same was registered as Metro Special Case No. 133 of 2007 and on 7-10-2007, Mahanagar Senior Special Judge, Dhaka took cognizance against the petitioner and co-accused Shah Alam Chowdhury and then transmitted the case record to the Senior Special Judge, Dhaka for trial who registered the same as Metro Bishesh Case No.133 of 2007. The case was then pending for framing of charge.

6. At this stage the petitioner moved this Division under Article 102 of the Constitution and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr. Rokon Uddin Mahmood, the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner after taking us with the petition, supplementary affidavit made exhaustive and strenuous argument touching upon various provisions of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2004 and its relevant Rules asserting that the instant proceeding against the petitioner is absolutely without jurisdiction and without any lawful authority being ex facie illegal and the same should be declared illegal and without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. He submits that the petitioner is a former Member of Parliament elected from the Constituency No.253 Chandina (Comilla -6) for two consecutive terms and a former Minister of State, Ministry of Liberation Welfare Affairs to the Government of Bangladesh. Apart from that the petitioner was holding the position of the Chairman of Bangladesh freedom Fighter's Central Council. Besides, he is a businessman of repute. His bone of contention is that out of malice and the instant case was initiated against the petitioner only to harass him and the allegation was prima facie baseless and, as such, no action should be taken against the petitioner upon the admitted position of the facts and circumstances of the case as well as the relevant laws on the issue.

8. Mr. Mahmood advances several arguments. He mainly contends that the ACC cannot submit a charge sheet in a case where it has not made an enquiry in accordance with provisions of chapter III of the Act. He has also assailed that an 'enquiry' as defined by Rule 2(Ka) of ACC rules is a condition precedent for filing a complaint by the ACC against a person in the Police Station for it to be investigated under section 20. Only after an enquiry has been made with the necessary approval as required under Chapter III of the ACC Rules, 2007 a complaint in police station can be made.

9. Next he submits that section 32 of the Act 2004 provides for two different and distinct sanctions sub-section (1) provides for sanction of ACC before cognizance is taken by a Court. In fact, sub-section 32(1) Prohibits a Court from taking cognizance without sanction of ACC and sub-section (2) provides for obtaining sanction before submission of the charge sheet. In this case as he submits cognizance was taken by the Special Judge on 17-7-2007, but there was no sanction under section 32(1) as required for taking cognizance by the Court. Such sanction for taking cognizance is separate, distinct and independent from the sanction required for submitting the charge sheet under section 32(2). Such sanction will not suffice to meet the requirement of Section 32(1), which is an independent sanction, and which is for the purpose of taking cognizance, whereas the sanction under section 32(2) of the Act 2004 is for a separate purpose, namely, submission of charge sheet. The sanction granted in Form 3 under Rule 15(7) of the Rules expressly stipulates that such sanction is for the submission of charge sheet. In no way can the said sanction be construed to read as a sanction required under section 32(1) for the purpose of taking cognizance by the Court.

10. Basing on these arguments on the point of sanction the learned Counsel further submits that the decision reported in Md Nazhnuddin Chairman vs Government of Bangladesh 61 DLR 2009 81 is not applicable in the instant case since the points argued in this case by the learned Counsel were not argued or decided in the said reported case. Substantiating his argument the learned Counsel emphatically submits that when section 32 was amended in April 2007 bringing in the requirement of sanction for taking cognizance in addition to sanction before submission of the charge sheet there was no corresponding amendment of the Rules. Therefore, the Rules do not contain any prescribed form for the sanction required for taking cognizance of the offence as prescribed by Section 32(1) and Form 3 is expressly and essentially for submission of the charge which has not prescribed any sanction for taking cognizance.

11. Mr Mahmood lastly argued since section 20 of the Act made an express provision in sub-section (2) authorizing delegation of its power to investigate to an officer of the Commission and accordingly the Commission has delegated its power for investigation to its officer by gazette notification which is absolutely a cram non judice, i.e. without jurisdiction. On this point he referred to the decision reported in 21 BLD (AD) 10 (Para-9) wherein it has been held :

"A member of the Election Commission acting as the Acting Chief Election Cornmissioner could not exercise the power of the Election Commission constituted under Article 118(1) of the Constitution in the absence of delegation of the power of the Commission for exercise by one of the members of the Commission. Such exercise of power of the Commission by one of its members was also found to be "Coram non juice without jurisdiction."

12. Mr Khorshed Alam Khan, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the Anti-Corruption Commission on the other hand, opposes the Rule and submits that all the submissions as advanced by the learned Senior Counsel Mr Rokanuddin Mahmood have been well addressed and Answered in the decision of ACC vs Mohiuddin Khan Alamgir 62 DLR (AD) 290 and 295, Habibur Rahman Mollah vs the State 62 DLR (AD) 233, and Md. Nazimuddin Chairman vs Government of Bangladesh 29 BLD 559. The ground of sanction Mr Khan submits that rule 15(7) of ACC Rules, 2007 provides that when a case is required to be filed under section 32 of the Act and a sanction has been accorded in that respect, it has been given in Form-3 of the Rule. Rule 15(4) of the ACC Rules, 2007 reasserts that only when charge sheet has to be filed before the Court, sanction is required and, as such, section 32 of the Act made it clear that no Court shall take cognizance of any case without such sanction. Hence, it cannot be said that sanction under section 32 of the Act submitted in Form-3 is not the only sanction contemplated under the entire Act and Rules. Moreover, the sanction is an administrative Act which is not subject to any judicial scrutiny and on that score he submits that the sanction in the instant case is an outcome of an administrative decision which is not a subject matter to be interfered with by any judicial scrutiny.

13. Referring to the case of Habibur Rahman Mollah vs State and another 62 DLR (AD) 233 Mr Khan argued that the allegations against the petitioner on the facts and circumstances of the case are absolutely disputed facts which can only be decided on evidence at the trial.

14. Be that as it may we have heard the learned senior Counsel for the petitioner and the learned Counsel for the respondent No.3 at length and considered their submissions carefully. We have gone through the petition, supplementary affidavit, supplementary affidavit and the respective Annexure filed with them carefully.

15. The first argument by the senior Counsel for the petitioner on the point of sanction has been well addressed by this Division in the case of Nazimuddin Chairman vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 29 BLD 559 where after discussing and interpreting section 32 of the Act 2004 (amended and unamended) and Rules 15(2)(4)(7) finally it was held :

"The impugned sanction is certainly a valid sanction and only sanction as contemplated under Rule '15(4) of ACC Rules, 2007 within the meaning of section 32(1)(2) of ACC Act 2007 and it is absolutely in keeping with the spirit of various provisions of law relevant for the purpose as discussed above. We, therefore, find substance in the contention of the learned Counsel for the respondent that no other sanctions of any kind have been prescribed under ACC, Act and Rules."

16. This view finds support in the case of ACC vs Dr Mohiuddin Khan Alamgir 62 DLR (AD) 290. His Lordship Justice ABM Khairul Haque on this point observed: "Under the above amended section, after completion of the investigation, the investigating officer, under sub-section (2) of section 32, on obtaining the sanction from the Commission, would submit the police report before the Court along with copy of the letter of sanction. The Court, under sub-section (1), would take cognizance, only when there is such sanction from the Commission. Both the sub-section 10 and sub-section (2) of the section 32 envisages only one sanction, not two. Sub-section (1) does not spell out or even envisage filing of any fresh sanction when the sanction to prosecute has already been filed along with the charge sheet of the investigating officer. It only envisages that without such sanction from the Commission (কমিশনের অনুমোদন ব্যতিরেকে) as spelt out in sub-section (2), no Court shall take cognizance of the offence (কোন আদালত এই আইনের অধীন কোন অপরাধ বিচারার্থ আমলে গ্রহন করিবে না।) under sub-section (1) of section 32."

His Lordship further observed:

"The High Court Division, however, on consideration sub-rule (7) of rule 15 of the দূর্নীতি দমন বিধিমালা, ২০০৭ (the Rules) held that sanction is required to be filed as the time of institution of the case (মামলা দায়েরের ক্ষেত্রে) on the erroneous understanding that sanction shall also be required at the time of lodging an first information report. But as a matter of fact, the Act as well as the Rules do not envisage lodging of any first information report but only a complaint (অভিযোগ) either under rule 3 or rule 4 of the Rules and no sanction is required to file any complaint."

<u>17. We do not think that there needs any further deliberation on the point of sanction as the same has been set at rest by this Division and the Appellate Division by now. We are also in agreement that the sanction as contemplated under section 32 of the Act is indeed an administrative Act which is not subject to any judicial scrutiny. We find support in this regard in the case of Bangladesh vs lqbal Hasan Mahmood CC Tuku 60 DLR (AD) 147 wherein his Lordship justice Md. Joynul Abedin (as his Lordship then was) observed that "the process of sanction is an administrative act and is not subject to any judicial scrutiny."</u>

18. In that case sanction accorded by NBR was challenged on the plea of coram non judice and his Lordship repelled the argument holding: "The next contention of Mr Ajmalul Hossain is that the sanction in the instant case is coramnonjudice as it was accorded by the NBR in its meeting presided over by its Chairman who was not a member of the Board and further, that the sanction is also bad in law as it was given without giving prior notice to the respondent has also no substance."

19. Therefore, the submission of Mr Mahmood that the power of delegation as per section 20 of ACC Act found to be corum non judice has no legs to stand.

20. Next comes the question whether the trial of the petitioner on the facts allegedly committed prior to promulgation of ACC Act can be sustained since at the relevant time ACC Act (দূর্নীতি দমন আইন ২০০৪) was not in the filed. Here we want to quote a pertinent portion from the judgment in the case of Habibur Rah Mollah vs State 62 DLR (AD) 233 wherein his Lordship justice SK Sinha while holding that allegation as discussed in the FIR in the said case can only be decided on evidence at the trial observed:

"Whether the appellant has disproportionate wealth, whether he has concealed his known source of income, whether there is disjoined of charges and whether the trial of the appellant on facts  allegedly committed prior to the promulgation of Durnity Daman Commission Ain,  2004 constitute an offence under the Durnity Daman Commission Ain are disputed facts can only be decided on  evidence at the trial.  This is not a case that the allegations as disclosed in the first Information report and the police report do not disclose any offence. If accepting the allegations made and charges leveled on their face value, the Court had come to the conclusion that no offence was disclosed, the matter would have been different. In view of the above, I am of the view that there is no legal impediment to proceed with the trial of the case"

21. His Lordship in holding the above view took into consideration the decisions of Akhtar Hossain Khan vs State 29 DLR (SC) 101, Mofazzal Hossain Mollah vs State, 45 DLR (AD) 175 Title Suit Baliah vs Title Suit Rangachari, AIR 1969 (SC) 701, and Md Nizamuddin vs State, 30 DLR 49 (FB), Abul Kalam Khan vs Riza Morshed 5 BLC 2000.

22. Upshot of all these decisions clearly echoed that the allegations against the petitioner shall have to be settled before the trial Court on evidence. Unequivocally all the decisions as discussed above held the same. All the points pressed into service by Mr Rokanuddin Mahmood can be decided at the trial on full fledged hearing after evidence both oral and documentary.

23. That being the position we refrain from making any deliberation whatsoever upon the rest of the submissions advanced on behalf of the petitioner. We also want to make it clear that whatever observations we have made in this judgment is only for a limited purpose i.e. only for disposal of this Rule and this should not have any bearing on the trial which is now pending before the Special Judge, Dhaka.

24. We, therefore, hold that this writ petition does not merit any substance which should be discharged outright.

25. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. However, during trial the petitioner shall continue on bail already granted to him by this Division.

The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated and recalled.

End.

full_judgment:
Sharif Uddin Chaklader J: This appeal by the defendant is directed against judgment and decree dated 17-3-2004 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka decreeing Title Suit No. 23 of 1995.

2. Respondent as plaintiff, instituted the aforesaid suit, for a decree, amongst other, declaring the deed of agreement dated 15-6-1993 in between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1-3 being deed No. 6944 for the year of 1993 registered in the office of the Sub-Registrar, Gulshan, Dhaka, stands cancelled and the earnest money paid thereunder has been lawfully forfeited, and direct defendant No. 15-6-1993 in his office. Plaintiff also prayed for declaring that the Power of Attorney executed by the plaintiff in favour of the defendant No. 1, deed No. 6945 for the year of 1993 and further declaring transfer permission in Memo No. RAJUK/ESTATE/270(2) Stha dated 25-1-1995 issued by Deputy Director (Estate), Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakha, Dhaka as void, ineffective, illegal and not binding on the plaintiff. Also for a decree for declaring any and all sale deed(s) executed and registered by defendant No. 1, purportedly on behalf of plaintiff, is/are of no legal effect and not binding on the plaintiff, a decree declaring plaintiffs right, title and possession in the schedule property, a decree for khas possession of the schedule property, a decree for permanent injunction upon defendant No. 1 not to execute any sale deed, decree for permanent injunction upon defendant No. 6 not to register any sale deed executed by defendant No. 1, a decree for permanent injunction upon defendant No. 5 not to mutate name pursuant to any deed of sale executed by defendant No. 1, a decree for mense profit and /or damages/ compensation for use and occupation of the schedule property.

3. It has been stated in the plaint that an agreement was arrived on 15-6-1993 in between the plaintiff and defendant No.1 with his minor sons, defendant No. 2 and 3, for transfer of the schedule property. In the deed of agreement it has been stipulated that consideration money is sum of Taka 1,30,00,000 (Taka One Crore Thirty Lakh) only, out of which Taka 40,00,000 (Taka Forty Lakh) only is paid by pay order No. 173456 dated 10-6-1993, issued by ANZ Grindlays Bank Plc to the plaintiff, the receipt of which was plaintiff acknowledges and admits. Balance consideration money at Taka 90,00,000 shall be paid by the defendant on or before 14-9-93 to the plaintiff and for the due payment of the said balance, delivers to the plaintiff a Bank guarantee issued by ANZ Grindlays Bank Plc, 2, Dilkusha Commercial Area, Dhaka guaranteeing payment of the balance aforesaid money on the 91st day after the date of execution of the agreement and if the defendant paid the said money by that date, thereupon be entitled to received one or more registered deeds of sale duly executed by the plaintiff. The plaintiff claimed that time was essence of the contract and it was fixed on 14-9-1993 as the date for payment of the balance of the purchase money. Plaintiff executed a Power of Attorney dated 15-6-1993 in favour of defendant No.1 to look after and manage the property and to present and obtain approval of building plans from Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakha, RAJUK for additions, alterations and changes to existing building and to make new buildings as attorney shall see fit, to seek and obtain from the necessary transfer permission for sale and transfer of the house, to sign whenever necessary and make the necessary payments on behalf of the plaintiff in respect of transfer fees and other charges and to do all other acts, deeds and things necessary or ancillary to the purpose. Power of Attorney, plaintiff stated that was not an Irrevocable Power of Attorney. This Power of Attorney, plaintiff stated, that no power was given to defendant No. 1 to execute and register sale deed personally and which is not passed through it. Plaintiff stated, defendant No. 1 failed to obtain the requisite transfer permission from RAJUK (defendant No. 5) within the stipulated 90 days. Aforementioned Bank guarantee given on 15-6-1993 was required to be extended and defendant No. 4, at the request of defendant No. 1, issued letter dated 12-9-1993 and addressed to the plaintiff, stating inter alia "This guarantee shall be valid up to TWELFTH DAY OF NOVEMBER, 1993 and all claims for payment must be made within the above date". Plaintiff stated that, aforesaid letter dated 12-9-1993 issued at the request of defendant No. 1, made material deviation from the original guarantee dated 15-6-1993 and by practicing fraud on the plaintiff, vitiating the entire transaction and rendering the Bank Guarantee ineffective. Plaintiff further stated that, in order to perpetuate fraud on the plaintiff, defendant No. 1 deliberately made delay in delivering the letter of extension of Bank Guarantee on the ground of defendant No. 1 heart ailment. Defendant No. 1's delay was actuated by malafide motive of delaying payment of the balance consideration money. In the circumstances, plaintiff stated that, he was not paid and has remained un-paid till date, the balance sum of Taka 90,00,000 which was to be paid on or before 14-9-93 to the plaintiff. Defendant No. 1 to 3 entered into physical possession of the schedule property and they are continuing as such till the present moment. Plaintiff through his learned lawyer issued legal notice dated 19-12-1994 addressed to the defendant No. 1, requesting him to make payment of the aforesaid balance consideration sum of Taka 90,00,000 failing which the said agreement shall be deemed cancelled without any further notice. Defendant No. 1 refused to accept the said legal notice. Thereafter, plaintiff issued the letter addressed to defendant No. 1 on 17-3-1994 terminating the agreement dated 15-6-1993, notified the earnest money has been forfeited. Plaintiff informed defendant No. 1 that Power of Attorney dated 15-6-1993 being deed No. 6945 for the year of 1993 revoked by the deed dated 14-3-1994 duly notarised in London and attested by the Bangladesh High Commission in United Kingdom. These facts, plaintiff informed to all the defendants including RAJUK by letter dated 17-3-1994 which was received by RAJUK on 9-4-1994 notifying cancellation/revocation of the power of Attorney who requesting by memo No. Raj UK/Estate/4002 Stha dated 27-9-1994 to plaintiff to appear before the Chairman, Rajuk, on 15-10-1994 to which, authorised person of the plaintiff, Mirza Mohammad Ali Ispahani, requested by letter dated 19-11-1994 for fixing for date for payment, which was received by defendant No. 5 on 22-11-1994 but no reply from the office of Deputy Director (Estates) was received instead defendant No. 5 issued transfer permission to defendant No. 1 and on the strength of the aforesaid Power of Attorney, which was cancelled, purportedly execute the sale deed and cause the same to be registered in the office of defendant No. 6.

4. It is further plaint case that, plaintiff was ready and willing on the date fixed to execute a proper deed of sale on receiving the balance of the purchase money and in fact called upon defendant No. 1 to perform his part of the contract and to pay the balance, of the purchase money on the date fixed,. but the defendant No. 1 with a malafide motive to delay payment of the balance consideration money thereby making unlawful and illegitimate gain for himself and causing loss to the plaintiff by practicing fraud on the plaintiff, requested defendant No. 4 to issue letter dated 12-9-93 containing material deviation as stated above having gone into possession, the defendant No. 1 to 3 are now preparing unlawfully and without lawful authority to execute and register sale deed in their favour despite cancellation of the aforesaid deed of agreement dated 15-6-1993 and revocation of Power of Attorney dated 15-6-1993. By reason of several defaults of defendant No. 1 the plaintiff has suffered damage.

5. Against the aforesaid reliefs as prayed by plaintiff, defendants have filed written statement on 27-7-1996. It is their case that, it is doubtful whether the plaintiff has filed actually the instant suit and also whether the Power of Attorney holder initiated the suit for getting power for filing.

6. It is the specific case of the defendants that no registered deed of agreement for sale between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 2 and 3 on 15-6-1993 was executed. The price money of the property in suit fixed at Taka 1,30,00,000 and Taka 40,00,000 has already been paid to the plaintiff as earnest money and thereafter, the balance of the consideration money of sum of taka 90,00,000 also been paid to the plaintiff as per terms of the said contract. It is further case of the defendants that, it was the legal and moral obligation of the plaintiff to execute and register the sale deed in normal course. It has further been stated that defendant No. 2-3 being vendees and having been put into possession in the property in suit by the plaintiff in part performance of the contract followed by a registered agreement, the defendants No. 2-3 cannot be ousted from their possession in as much as, they have acquired an indefeasible right over the said property and the plaintiff vendor has lost all his right to the property. It is further case of defendants No. 2-3, as principal defendants in this suit, having a registered agreement for sale in respect of the suit property in their favour accompanied by possession in part performance of the contract, their possession is absolutely lawful and they have a right over the property in suit and such right cannot be made a subject matter of interference and no decree for permanent injunction, as sought for in the suit, can be claimed by the plaintiff, either in law or in equity.

7. It is further stated that, defendants performed their part of the contract fully in strict accordance with the terms of the contract and the full consideration as shown in the deed of agreement has been paid to the plaintiff within the stipulated time. Defendant further stated that, plaintiff has deliberately refrained himself from mentioning the words of the said sale and transfer after the word purpose while describing clause 5 of the contract. It was intended by the parties that upon full payment of consideration, plaintiff will personally execute and register the sale deed in favour of defendant No. 1 and 2. It is further been stated that appointing defendant No. 1 as attorney to do and execute things and deeds in pursuance of the contract and got the said power of Attorney registered, it was obvious intention of the parties that the said power of attorney would never be revoked. Defendant further stated that, plaintiff himself under his own signature made an application to the Director (Estates) Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakha, Dhaka on 15-6-1993 seeking permission for transfer of the property in suit in favour of these defendants Nos. 2 and 3 and by another letter of the said date addressed to the said Director plaintiff informed him that he appointed defendant No. 1, Md. Abdur Rouf Chowdhury as his lawfully constituted attorney by a registered deed and in the said letter the specimen signature of defendant No. 1 was also given and his attested photograph was attached. Thereafter, RAJUK, proforma defendant No. 5 upon consideration of the merits of the case, approved the application for transfer of the suit property in its meeting No. 1/94 dated 28-2-1994 and the minutes of the said meeting was duly confirmed in Meeting No. 2/94 dated 31-3-1994. The proforma defendant No. 5 thereafter, for reasons known to them, gave a letter under reference No. RAJUK/Estate/4001 STHA dated 27-9-94 seeking further information and documents. Defendant No. 1 as lawfully constituted attorney of the plaintiff gave a reply to the said letter on 13-10-94 giving all details regarding the sale transaction and complied with the requirements of the RAJUK and presented all original documents to RAJUK in person and photo copies of the relevant documents viz. Power of Attorney, lease agreement of RAJUK and approved plan and all receipts, showing payment of Municipal Taxes, Gas, water and Electricity Bills and solicited an early action in the matter. RAJUK, proforma defendant No. 5, asked the plaintiff, the original lessee and his constituted attorney, the principal defendant No. 1, to appear personally or through their representatives before the Member, Estates with all their documents by 15-10-94. The principal defendant No.1 appeared before the Member, Estate with all relevant papers and documents but the plaintiff did not appear. Defendants thereafter, stated that, it will appear from the proceedings of the General Meeting No. 7/94 held on 23-10-94 of the RAJUK that the plaintiff informed RAJUK about the alleged cancellation of the power of attorney by him but he failed to produce the alleged instrument of cancellation and, as such, the plaintiffs prayer for stay of proceedings was not accepted by RAJUK. Thereafter, defendants stated that, as attorney of the plaintiff, thereafter, wrote a letter to the Director (Estate) RAJUK on 20th December, 1994 requesting him for permission to transfer the property in the name of the purchasers in pursuance of the deed of agreement for sale to which, the Director (Estate) by the letter No. RAJUK/Estate/144 STHA dated 12-1-95 directed the principal defendant No. 1 to deposit a sum of Taka 15,60,889 only as transfer fee and a further sum of Taka 5,360 only as service charges from 31-12-90 to 31-12-94, by 15-2-95. Defendant No. 1 by letter dated 15-1-95 addressed to the Director (Estate) informed him that the service charges being a sum of Taka 5360 was already deposited on 22-11-1994 and transfer fee of Taka 15,60,889 was deposited on 15-11-990 with Janata Bank, DIT Branch, Dhaka and the payment receipt dated 22-11-1994 and 15-1-1995 were also forwarded to him. Thereafter, RAJUK gave transfer permission to the principal defendant No. 1 as the constituted attorney of the plaintiff by letter dated 25-1-95.

8. On the averment with regard to the validity of Bank Guarantee up to 20th November, 1993 it is stated that it is however, a matter of record. This defendant submits in this connection that on the request of Rahima Food Corporation on account of defendant No. 1, ANZ Grindlays bank by its letter dated 9th November, 1993 revalidated the Bank Guarantee upto 20th February, 1993. As a matter of fact, the aforesaid revalidation of the Bank Guarantee was not at all necessary in as much as the entire price of the suit property was already paid to the plaintiff by that time as under:—

(a) Draft No. 173456 dated 10-6-93 for Taka 40,00,000 already acknowledged by the plaintiff in the deed of agreement.

(b) Draft No. 01729392 dated 9-6-92 for US Dollars 2,00,000 equivalent to Taka 90,00,000 to the plaintiff on 24-6-93 when there was no agreement.

(c) Cash payment of Taka 3,25,000 by receipt No. 136 dated 15-6-93. The original Bank Guarantee dated 15-6-93 for Taka 90,00,000 was renewed upto 12th September, 1993 and again up to 9th November, 1993 at the instance of the defendants in good faith without knowledge that the plaintiff had already collected US Dollar 2,00,000 from the ANZ Grindlays Bank on 24th June, 1993.

9. The defendant thereafter claimed that plaintiff has already paid up the balance consideration money as such this suit having filed with further claim as such, exemplary cost as per section 35A of the Code of Civil Procedure may be awarded upon plaintiff upon dismissing the suit.

Learned Judge framed the following issues as:—

১। অত্র মোকদ্দমা বর্তমান আকারে ও প্রকারে চলিতে পারে কি না।

২। অত্র মোকদ্দমার কারন আছে কি না।

৩। অত্র মোকদ্দমায় বাদীপক্ষ প্রার্থীত মতে ডিক্রী পাইতে হকদার কি না।

৪। বাদী আর কি কি প্রতিকার পাইতে পারে।

Both the sides examined two witnesses each.

10. Learned Judge on consideration of materials on record and depositions of the witnesses decreed the suit.

11. Learned Judge found that, the suit is not barred by limitation and not bad for defect of parties. On consideration of Exhibit Kha i.e. the deed of agreement for sale the learned Judge found that it admitted receipt of Taka 40,00,000 and it is acknowledged by the plaintiff. In respect of balance consideration of money at Taka 90,00,000 to be paid on or before 14-9-93, the learned Judge found that, the said money was not paid within time stipulated and since the defendant claimed that he paid balance consideration money of Taka 90,00,000 facts of payment of 90,00;000 lies upon the defendant ,and held that defendants failed to prove the, said fact. On the Bank Guarantee dated 10-11-9, Exhibit-8, the learned Judge found that "it appears that the original Bank Guarantee issued on 15-6-1993 but the terms "upon execution of one or more registered deed of sale" was newly inserted in letter issued on 12-11-93. It is also proved by letter dated 9-11-93 the validity of the Bank Guarantee was extended up to 20th day of February, 1994. 18. TH Khan filed an amended written statement. It appears from the amended written statement that it in fact amended certain statements made in the original written statement filed on 9-2-1995. Let us see this written statement, "The defendant No. 1-3 filed written statement on 27 July 1996 in order to contest this suit and establishing Defendant's case.

19. The defendant's case is that full consideration money for purchase of the suit property was paid by defendant No. 1 within the period stipulated in the sale agreement. The payment of Taka 90,00,000 was made by the Defendant through Bank Draft No. 01729393 dated 9-6-1992 drawn by ANZ Bank PLC, London, for USD 2,00,000 (Bank Draft) which has been equivalent to Taka 90,00,000 (applying conversion rate of US $ 1 = Taka 45).

20. At the time when the trial Court heard this case and delivered its judgment certain facts although known to the Defendants which were alleged but the evidence in support of these facts were unobtainable despite Defendant's diligent and reasonable efforts to obtain the same. The defendant tried to obtain those documents supporting the facts which he requested from ANZ Grindlays Bank in relation to the payment of the Bank Draft. But the evidence in support of these facts could not be retrieved at the time of the trial. Nevertheless, the documents recently received from ANZ Grindlays Bank supporting the facts alleged by the defendants are proved."

21. The learned Advocate relied on several decisions i.e. the case of Jadav Chandra vs Abdul Khaleque, 27 DLR (AD) 114, the case of Abul Kalam vs Sunhar Ali, 46 DLR (AD) 130, the case of Abdul Latif vs Aisha Bibi, 25 DLR 108, the case of Parsotim vs Lal Mohar, AIR 1931 PC 143, the case of Madan Mohan vs Munnibai, AIR 1957 Nag 15, the case of Radha Krishna vs Dwaraka Das, 36 DLR (AD) 253, the case of Keramat Ali vs Yunus, 15 DLR (SC) 120, the case of Sagarmal vs Annpurna, AIR 1964 Pat 298 and the case of Montazullah vs Farasatullah, 26 DLR 31 in support of his case for considering the present written statement.

22. We have considered all these decisions.

23. The case of Jadav Chandra vs Abdul Khaleque, 27 DLR (AD) 114, is a case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, where plaint was sought to be amended as; 'Since a co-sharer tenant of non-agricultural land is entitled to apply for preemption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, it does not appear how the nature and character of the application can be said to be altered by substitution of a new case altogether by reason of the amendment prayed for. Whatever changes were sought to be made were changes in form and not in substance. The learned Judges were not justified in rejecting the prayer for amendment of the application upon the view they took.

24. Moreover, since the relief prayed for could be given by the Court under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, even if that section had not been specifically mentioned in the application, it was not necessary either to apply for amendment for a change of description in the cause title.

25. The case of Abul Kalam Azad vs Sunhar Ali, 46 DLR (AD) 130 where the written statement was sought to be amendment after long lapse of time. The Court held as; Amendment of a plaint and amendment of a written statement are not governed by exactly the same principle. The defendant would not be allowed to introduce an alternative and completely different kind of defence which will have the effect of introducing a new controversy between the parties.

26. The case of Abdul Latif vs Ashia Bibi 25 DLR 108 where on the admissibility of additional evidence under rule 27 Order XLI CPC, the Court held as; Where fresh evidence to fill up a gap in the record is discovered pending appeal in circumstances which if no appeal was pending, would have given the party a right to apply for review under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code, the proper course for the party (a review being out of question) is to apply for the admission of additional evidence either under the general principles of law or under the specific provision of Order XLI, rule 27 which lays down that the appellate Court may for any other substantial cause (viz. other than those particularly specified) allow such evidence or documents to be produced or witness to be examined.

27. The case of Parsotim Thakur vs Lal Mohar Thakur AIR 1931 PC 143, a case on additional evidence under Order XLI, rule 27, CPC, the Court held as; The provisions of Section 107 as elucidated by Order XLI, rule 27, are clearly not intended to allow a litigant who has been unsuccessful in the lower Court to patch up the weak parts of his case and fill up omissions in the Court of appeal. Under Rule 27, C1. (1)(b) it is only where, the appellate Court "requires" it (i.e. finds it needful) that additional evidence can be admitted. It may be required to enable the Court to pronounce judgment, or for any other substantial cause, but in either case it must be the Court that requires it. The legitimate occasion for the exercise of this discretion is not whenever before the appeal is heard a party applies to adduce fresh evidence, but "when on examining the evidence as it stands, some inherent lacuna or defect becomes apparent". It may well be that the defect may be pointed out by a party, or that a party may move the Court to apply the defect, but the requirement must be the requirement of the Court upon its appreciation of evidence as it stands. Wherever the Court adopts this procedure it is bound by Rule 27(2) to record its reasons for so doing, and under Rule 29 must specify the points to which the evidence is to be confined and record on its proceedings the points so specified. The power so conferred upon the Court by the Code ought to be very sparingly exercised, and one requirement at least of any new evidence to be adduced should be that it should have a direct and important bearing on a main issue in the case.

28. The case of Madan Mohan vs Munnibai, AIR 1957 Nag 15, where for taking additional evidence under order XLI Rule 27 CPC, the Court held as; The deposit of the money in the execution to which we referred was not made by Shree but by his widow Munnibai, and it is obvious such action is easy to manipulate if evidence in benami transaction is needed. If we were to this evidence we would have to try the issue and the plaintiff would be required to prove there was no collusion or fraud involved in the application by Munnibai to get the sale set-aside. We think that a fresh trial cannot granted in this case.

29. We are also of opinion that the substantive won by the decree-holder in the present case be set at naught merely by reason of an averment which requires detailed examination and strict in 1952, long after the decision of the learned Judge, and we do not think that it can affect substantive rights without its being made retrospect before it can be accepted. The new rule was either expressly or by necessary intendment. The intendment is not apparent upon the face of them and we do not think, that the new rule is application to this case.

30. The case of Radha Krishna vs Dwaraka Das, 36 DLR (AD) 253 where upon a suit originally filed for declaration of rights and for accounts-By a subsequent prayer an additional ground namely for dissolution of the firm was sought to be included in the suit-Question arose whether the amendment sought would alter the nature of the suit so as to substitute one cause of action for another cause in the suit and whether such an amendment of the plaint may be considered, the Court held as; All rules of Court are nothing but provisions intended to secure the proper administration of justice, and it is therefore essential that they should be made to serve and be sub-ordinate to that purpose, so that full powers of amendment must be enjoyed and should always be liberally exercised, but nonetheless no power has yet been given to enable one distinct cause of action to be substituted for another, nor to change by means of amendment the subject matter of the suit.

31. Amendments of the pleadings are allowed, even when a legal right accrued to the other party, if special circumstances of the case outweigh such consideration. In exercising this power, the Court would, no doubt, be reluctant to allow such an amendment, which would have the effect of totally altering nature of the suit, or take away a valuable right accrued by lapse of time, but where in the circumstances of the particular case, it would be plainly inequitable to refuse such a relief, the Court will not hesitate to act.

32. The case of Keramat Ali vs Md Yunus Hazi, 15 DLR (SC) 120, where the amendment of the plaint was allowed before the Supreme Court on the finding that, 'The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council consistently maintained that it had undoubtedly full power to allow amendments even where a legal right had accrued by lapse of time if the special circumstances of the case outweighed such considerations.

<u>33. In exercising this power no doubt, the Supreme Court, would be reluctant to allow an amendment which would have the effect of totally altering the nature of the suit or of taking away a valuable right accrued by lapse of time, but where in the circumstances of a particular case it would be plainly inequitable to refuse such a relief this Court will not hesitate to do what the Judicial Committee did.</u>

<u>34. The case of Sagarmal vs SMT Annpurna AIR 1964 Pat 298, where the suit was under Houses and rent suit under Bihar (lease, Rent and Eviction) Control (Amendment) Act, 1955 where additional evidence were considered under order XLI Rule 27 CPC as; Where additional evidence came into existence some time after the disposal of the suit, the appellate Court would be justified in admitting the additional evidence even at the appellate stage, if the Court thinks that but for the additional evidence there would remain some inherent lacuna and defect in the evidence made available before the trial Court.</u>

35. Lastly the case of Mantazullah vs Farasatullah 26 DLR 31 where the case for taking additional evidence at the appellate stage, the Court held as;

'The main question being as to whether M signed the miscellaneous application for pre-emption necessitates acceptance of these documents in accordance with law for pronouncing judgment and doing proper justice in the case. Therefore, these documents may be accepted on proper proof in accordance with law but it is not possible to do so in this Court as it will require oral evidence. The prayer for giving additional evidence in accordance with law having been allowed, justice demands that reasonable opportunity should be given to the respondent-opposite party to adduce rebuttable evidence, if any.

36. Excepting the case of Abul Kalam Azad vs Sunhar Ali, where the written statement was sought to be amendment, all the other cases are on amendment of the pleadings of plaint and on taking additional evidence. In that cited decision, the aspects of the decision was amendment of written statement, after long lapse of time as the suit was started on 6-12-86 after filing of the written statement, amendment of the written statement was filed by the defendant after close of evidence which the High Court Division allowed but the Appellate Division held that:—

"It may be pointed out here that the real question in controversy in the suit was eviction of a monthly tenant on the ground of default and sub-letting, whereas the issues raised in the amendment of the written statement were payment of salami of Taka 65,000 in respect of the premises on a permanent basis and also the story of incurring an expense of Taka 1,75,000 for the purpose of reconstruction of the damage building. In this case the original written statement was filed much earlier and after a long lapse of time the application for amendment of the written statement was filed. It is to be borne in mind that the amendment of a plaint and the amendment of the written statement are not governed by exactly the same principle. In the case reported in 26 DLR 205 the governing consideration was that an application to amend the written statement can be allowed if it is necessary to determine the real controversy between the parties, unless this test is satisfied the amendment cannot be allowed. It seems that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division on the material on records as available in the present case failed to appreciate the real issue involved the amendment."

37. The Appellate Division further held that "it may be mentioned here that the learned Single Judge, of course, observed in his judgment that there is inordinate delay in filing this application for amendment of the written statement but he allowed this by holding that the same can be compensated by giving money and consequently awarded cost of Taka 1000 as compensation to the plaintiffs. It must be stated here that the principle guiding the amendment of the written statement as contemplated under the law has not been taken note of and the learned Single Judge allowed these revision cases taking a sympathetic view in the matter which is not permitted by law. Thus, considering the entire facts and circumstances of the case and the law governing the amendment of the written statement, we are of the view that the orders passed by the learned Single Judge need to be set-aside. Since we are setting-aside the order of amendment of the written statement, the other order relating of P.W. 1 is necessary set-aside. Accordingly, both the appeals are allowed."

38. Appellants in the instant case wanted to armed the written statement filed on 27-7-1996, on 24-2-2010, long after 14 years, after closing of evidence, is squarely fallen within the dictum of the decision 46 DLR (AD)130. Order VIII of CPC governed filing of written statement. Order VIII CPC nowhere provide for filing of an additional written statement which negate the earlier written statement bringing on record almost a new case which surprise the plaintiff as plaintiff against the additional written statement in not in a position to controvert the same as CPC does not provide him so. Original written statement was filed on 27-7-1996 and it is sought to be amended on 24.2.2010 i.e. almost 15 years of filing of original written statement. Relying on the cited decision of Mr. Khan, i.e. the case of Abul Kalam vs Sunhar Ali, 46 DLR(AD) 130 we rejected the prayer for amendment of written statement.

39. On the merit of the case. It is the case of defendants that they have paid the entire consideration money as they paid US $ 2 lakh equivalent to Taka 90,00,000 to the plaintiff on 9-6-1992 on the basis of a loan from Mr. Abdul Matin Chowdhury of London who happens to be the brother-in-law of principal defendant No. 1.
